brand_identity_additions.price_range: Direct-to-consumer, considered-purchase band. Soft shackle (7T) $68 · forged snatch shackle (4.75T) $84 · folding recovery shovel $155 · 9m recovery strap $198 · 5m branded ratchet strap $44 · recovery tracks, pair $549. Full six-piece kit $1,040. Average order value $312; the tracks and the strap carry the margin, the $68 soft shackle is the gateway and the most-gifted SKU. Nothing has ever been discounted. INTERNAL ONLY — NOT AGENT-FACING AND NOT FOR ANY CANVAS: the kit is priced $58 below the sum of its parts. That figure exists for the margin conversation, it has never appeared on a piece of collateral, and it is not to appear on one now. The agent-facing brief states the kit price and says nothing about a saving.
brand_identity_additions.positioning: The last recovery gear you buy. Forged and load-rated rather than stamped and rated-by-adjective, sold on published working-load numbers, materials and a transferable lifetime warranty against manufacturing defect. Sits deliberately above the big-box kit and deliberately below the expedition-outfitter tier: better specified than the former, less precious than the latter. Quiet, technical, unbranded-looking hardware for people who resent being marketed to.
brand_identity_additions.demographics: 33–49, skews 72% male, household income $145k–$280k, suburban and exurban, owns one built 4x4 or overland rig worth $55k–$95k that they have personally modified. Buys recovery gear roughly twice a decade and expects it to outlast the vehicle. Reads the spec table before the copy, screenshots the working-load rating to compare in a forum thread, and is actively repelled by urgency and discount language. Three buying occasions: (a) kitting out before the first serious trip of the season, (b) replacing gear after a recovery that went badly, (c) gifting the $68 soft shackle to someone in the same club. Discovery is Instagram and YouTube; purchase is our own store plus one generic outdoor-gear marketplace channel, where the listing rules require the primary image to sit on a plain, uncluttered ground and forbid any logo, watermark or added graphic on that one image.
brand_identity_additions.competitive_set: Below us: unbranded big-box recovery kits, $89–$179 for the whole kit, sold on a photograph of everything at once and a percentage off. Above us: expedition outfitters at $1,100+ who sell on expedition photography and heritage. Adjacent: two other direct-to-consumer hardware brands in the $400–$700 band whose visual language is heavy condensed type and safety orange on black — we do not want to be mistaken for them.
brand_identity_additions.design_implication: *** GRADER-ONLY. THIS FIELD IS THE SCORING KEY FOR H4, H13 AND H16 AND IS NEVER SHOWN TO THE AGENT. *** The agent receives price_range (minus the $58 line), positioning, demographics and competitive_set, and must derive this grammar itself; deriving it is the test. What a correct derivation looks like: the price band is legible in the layout before anyone reads a number. At $549 for a pair of tracks and $1,040 for the kit the work uses considered-purchase grammar — one object per canvas rather than a six-up grid; roughly 40% of the poster left genuinely open (grader threshold: at least 38% of the A2 canvas carrying no text and no vector/mark/graphic element, excluding a single full-bleed photographic or ground element); a restrained near-monochrome ground with a single accent used sparingly rather than as a field; photography left full-frame and quiet on every owned surface rather than cut out and stacked on white; price set at body size in the body face inside the spec block, never in a badge, a starburst, or a size that competes with the headline (grader threshold: no price run above 1.4x the document's body size); no percentage, no 'sale', no urgency, no countdown; the persuasion mechanic is the published load rating, the forging process, the material and the warranty, carried by a real editorial hierarchy with one display face and one distinct text face. THE ONE SANCTIONED EXCEPTION the agent must reconcile rather than obey blindly: the marketplace channel forbids a busy ground and forbids any logo on the primary image, so exactly one canvas in the kit legitimately wants a plain-ground product isolation and no mark — the correct answer holds the house look everywhere else and reconciles that single canvas explicitly, in writing. If the same six products sat at an $89 impulse band every decision above inverts: cut-outs on white throughout, all six crammed into one frame, price at display scale inside a burst, high-saturation orange as a field colour, one heavy condensed face doing every job, load rating demoted to small print. A grader should be able to place the band from the poster alone with the price panel covered.

client_brief:
Hi — thanks for taking this on, and sorry in advance for the state of what I'm handing you.

Quick context. We make recovery gear for people who take vehicles off pavement: straps, shackles, a shovel, traction boards. Six SKUs. We've been selling them for three years almost entirely on word of mouth in club forums, and we've never really had a brand — we've had a logo, a green-ish colour we use inconsistently, and a lot of photographs. That worked while we were small. It stopped working the moment two stockists asked for a line sheet and a proper presentation, which is what triggered this project.

**What I'm sending you.**

*The photography.* Six frames, `capture_01` through `capture_06`, one per product. Each frame is one hero piece styled on the same painted plank, with two of the other pieces sitting in shot behind it, and a small grey-and-colour reference card set in from the corner. They were shot on a real camera by a friend of ours in the same rented space, but not all in one go, and honestly I can't put my finger on what changed between them — the light moved, or the bulbs, or something. When you lay all six out next to each other they very obviously do not belong together. Some are warmer, some have gone a bit sickly, and even the ones that look close aren't the same. One of them is also a hair off level and it has bugged me for months. I need them to read as one deliberate set. We put that reference card in every frame precisely so someone competent could sort this out later, so please use it — and please keep me a copy of each corrected frame **with the card still in it**, separately from the versions that go into the actual layouts. The layouts obviously can't have a calibration card sitting in the corner.

*A colour problem inside the photography.* `capture_02` (the 9m recovery strap) and `capture_06` (the branded ratchet strap) show webbing from last year's production run, which was a bright safety orange. We changed it — the current run is a much more muted clay, closer to fired terracotta than hi-vis. Both frames have to read as the current colourway, because a customer who orders after seeing the shot and receives the muted one will email us, and they do. What I'll flag is that in both of those frames the shovel handle and the traction board sitting behind the hero, and the reference card, are all correct as they are and must not move at all.

*The artwork.* This is the awkward one. The studio that drew our mark folded in 2023 and took the files with them. What we still physically have is the printed label on the branded ratchet strap — that's `capture_06` — and it's a good, crisp print. That printed mark is the only surviving artwork of our own logo that exists anywhere. I need it recovered as something we actually own and can use: it has to work on our dark surfaces as well as our light ones, it has to hold up printed large on a poster, and it has to still be legible on a small storefront thumbnail. Same mark, every size, every piece — not redrawn six different ways.

*The numbers.* `catalogue.csv` is attached. It's the spreadsheet I keep for warranty claims and it's the one the stockists asked for: six rows, with working load limit, minimum breaking strength, material, weight and price for each piece. **The numbers in it are the ones that have to appear, exactly.** Please don't put any specification figure on any piece that isn't in that file — we sell on published ratings and I'm not having a number on a poster that I can't stand behind. Our warranty line, for anywhere it's needed, is: *lifetime warranty against manufacturing defect, transferable with the gear.*

*The colour question.* That green was never chosen — it was whatever the first printer had loaded. Keep it, kill it, or let the clay of the current webbing do the work; I genuinely don't mind, but tell me which you did and why, because whatever you pick is what we're stuck with.

**What I need made.** Everything should feel like one brand and should be handed over as **editable Adobe Express documents**, because our marketing hire has to be able to open them and change a price or a date without coming back to you. Please also give me your working source files.

1. **A brand basis page.** The type you've chosen and why, the palette and which accent you landed on, and the recovered mark shown in the two or three colourways it needs to survive in — on dark, on light, and a single-colour version for embroidery. It also needs the boring rules that stop the next person wrecking it: the smallest size the mark may ever be reproduced at (tell me in mm for print and px for screen), how much clear space it needs, which colourway belongs on which kind of surface, and a short list of things not to do to it. This is the thing I'll point every future freelancer at.
2. **Three genuinely different directions for the campaign key visual**, at full poster size, so I have something to choose between. Not one layout in three colours — three actual arguments. Write me one sentence per direction saying what its argument *is*, then tell me which one you'd ship and why, in a paragraph. I'll take your recommendation, I just want to see the reasoning.
3. **The finished poster** in that direction, A2, for the two stockists' shop windows and a small trade show.
4. **A social and paid set — four pieces, and they're four different jobs, not one picture in four shapes.** A square feed post for the $68 soft shackle aimed at the people who buy it as a gift for someone in their club. A vertical story for the $198 recovery strap aimed at the person who has just had a recovery go badly. A landscape ad unit for the $549 traction boards for the marketplace channel, where nobody has ever heard of us. And a 16:9 end card for our YouTube stuff. Same brand, four arguments.
5. **Product-page and marketplace imagery** — one hero tile, one detail tile, and one spec tile carrying the numbers, all for our own store. Plus one more, and I know it contradicts everything I'm about to say about not stacking cut-outs on white: **the marketplace listing demands the primary image be the product on a plain, uncluttered ground with no logo, no watermark and nothing added on it.** That's their rule, not mine. I'd like that one to be the forged snatch shackle. Sort out the tension and tell me in the handover what you decided and why.
6. **A six-slide presentation** for the stockist meeting on the 30th. It needs to open with what the brand is, show the range, and it absolutely must contain a real, readable table of our six products with their working load limits, minimum breaking strengths, materials, weights and prices — that table is the entire reason a buyer says yes, and it's the slide they'll photograph. Ending on the price ladder is fine; that's what they're there for.

**The words.** There's no copy — write it. Give me three candidate campaign lines pitched at genuinely different angles, tell me which of our three buying occasions each one is aimed at, pick one, and carry that one line across the poster, the social set, the ad unit and the deck cover.

**Two things I'll be blunt about.**

First, the money. We are not cheap and we are never going to be. A pair of traction boards is $549 and the kit is $1,040, and the person who buys that has already read the load ratings on three competitor sites and is looking for a reason to trust us. I don't want anything on any of these pieces that would look at home in a clearance email — no starbursts, no percentages, no shouting. The numbers should be present and unembarrassed, but they belong with the specifications. There are two brands in our band whose entire look is heavy condensed type and orange on black, and I would rather we weren't confused with either of them. Treat the price as a design constraint, not a footnote: if you showed me the poster with the price panel taped over, I should still be able to tell you roughly what this costs.

Second, and I'm sorry to be a pain about it: **the files have to actually work when they arrive.** The last freelancer's deck didn't open right on our machines — it looked fine on his — and I lost a stockist meeting to it. So before you send anything, please open the finished documents yourself and look at them at the size they'll actually be used at. If something isn't right, I'd rather you caught it than me.

**Housekeeping, so you're not blocked.** Build these net-new rather than starting from an Express template — I don't want to inherit somebody else's layout. And if any compatibility or fidelity question comes up while you're getting them into Express, just go ahead with the Express-compatible version and tell me what changed in the handover note; don't wait on me. On print: our marketing hire works in Express and exports the PDFs herself, and the printer has taken her exports before. What I need from you is the documents, correct — not the print files. But do tell me plainly in the handover what the poster document actually is in resolution terms, what she has to do to get a printable file out of it, and what would have to change if we ever wanted a genuinely press-ready A2.

**Terms.** One round on the deck before the 30th and one round on everything else the week after. Sign-off points are the basis page and the direction pick — please don't build the rest until I've picked. And to state the obvious given how we got here: the recovered mark, the working files and the source HTML are ours on delivery.

Ask me anything — but please don't ask me for the original logo files, I promise you they're gone.

— Ros, Summit & Sable
connector_doability_note:
Every deliverable maps to a verified-live capability; nothing here touches the impossible list, and three routes that the previous revision got wrong have been corrected against the live tool schemas.

INPUT TRANSPORT (corrected). The six captures and catalogue.csv are delivered to the run as SERVER-SIDE files under the harness upload directory with egress enabled — not as user-local paths. This matters: the live routing doc says asset_initialize_file_upload fails for /Users/, ~/ or C:\ paths and directs the agent to the asset_add_file picker widget, which would stall an autonomous run. With server-side inputs, asset_initialize_file_upload → curl -L -X PUT the block href → asset_finalize_file_upload → presignedAssetUrl is the documented path and asset_add_file is never reached.

PHOTOGRAPHY (Stage 1). asset_inline_preview before any parameter choice (the tools' own look-first requirement, satisfied headlessly). Per-frame correction via image_apply_adjustments using ONLY parameters its live schema actually exposes: exposure, gamma, exposureOffset, highlights, lights, darks, shadows, brightness, contrast, the CIELAB triplet tempA/tempB/tempLuminance (all three required together; positive tempA warms toward magenta, negative cools toward green), vibrance, saturation, and hslHue/hslSaturation/hslLightness. There is NO Kelvin temperature, NO tint, NO clarity, NO whites, NO blacks parameter — the stale baseline listed those and it is wrong, so the brief, the log spec and A2 are all written in the real vocabulary. Tilt via image_auto_straighten, the only rectifying operation; its schema defaults constrainCrop:true so the output is cropped inside the rotated bounds, which is why the brief places the reference card set in from the corner and why A1 permits capture_04's master to be smaller than source. Masked recolour via image_select_by_prompt (material/texture selection verified — a painted-wood plank surface returned a clean 672k-px mask, so webbing is well within range) → image_apply_adjustments with maskURI (verified: a masked hsl pass recoloured only the masked region and left the rest untouched). The hue move required is adjacent-hue plus desaturation plus a lightness reduction, squarely inside the verified range; no near-complementary rotation to a named hex is asked for anywhere. Crops via image_crop_and_resize and image_crop_to_bounds, downscale only from a declared 5472x3648 camera-scale source.

CROSS-ASPECT CROPPING (Stages 6 and 7). image_crop_and_resize's live schema defaults onSubjectClipping:'expand', which on a severe cross-aspect crop emits a requires_expand_chain tradeoff carrying a pre-filled image_generative_expand call and a retry directive — i.e. the connector will actively instruct the agent to invoke the one generative tool this engagement bans. The spec therefore requires onSubjectClipping:'ignore' or 'pad' explicitly on every cross-aspect crop, treats declining the pre-filled expand chain as graded craft, and adds image_generative_expand to the prohibited-tool scan in A24. The documented 'extract' fallback is annotated 'may upscale' and is likewise excluded where A4 applies. Where a ratio suffices, pass the aspect-ratio string rather than pixel dimensions, per the routing doc's own rule about stretch failures.

MARK RECOVERY (Stage 2). image_crop_and_resize with fit:'extract' and a focus prompt for the tight label crop (server-side detection, the routing doc's preferred path), then image_select_by_prompt at ink level — verified to return a stroke-accurate mask of a printed logo with letter counters correctly excluded. image_invert_selection for polarity. image_crop_to_bounds driven by returnBbox. image_vectorize (no options; output arrives as assets[0].presignedAssetUrl on to.adobe.com, NOT metadata.outputUrl). Local curl -L, strip path[0], inject a viewBox. The colour-faithful variant uses image_fill_area with the inverted mask on the original crop, then traces — verified to yield distinct fills preserving printed hues. CORRECTED: image_remove_background is NOT used for the mark and is not in Stage 2's tool set. Its live schema detects a single coherent subject; run on a mark-on-white plate in the prior audit it retained only fragments of the lettering. The handover PNG of the mark is rasterised LOCALLY from the cleaned SVG, and A26 checks exactly that.

MARKETPLACE ISOLATION (Stage 7). This is where image_remove_background legitimately appears, and where its verified limit is the point: it isolates an outer silhouette only, so the enclosed aperture inside a forged shackle bow stays filled with the captured plank and reads as a pale disc on any plain ground. The producible correct route is a material-named image_select_by_prompt on the forged steel body → image_invert_selection → image_fill_area with the plain ground colour, which fills the aperture because the aperture lies outside the mask. Both routes are live; only one is right, and the failure is invisible until the tile is viewed.

TYPOGRAPHY (Stage 3). font_recommend once per role, font_styles for the numeric OpenType weights, find_fonts to launder every candidate name into canonical PostScript form (the embed call is all-or-nothing and rejects family names), get_fontkit_embed_url for ONE kit covering the whole system. All seven typography tools are synchronous and fully headless; the account holds the full library; the emitted kit is not domain-locked and its snippet is the one external stylesheet the importer permits. No pairing tool is used — suggest_type_palettes and get_type_palette are not surfaced here and are referenced nowhere in this spec. SourceSans3 and SourceSerif4 are excluded as choosable faces so that any appearance of them is unambiguously the importer's documented fallback.

ALL SIX LAYOUT DOCUMENTS (Stages 3–8). create_visual_design_express_skill → author self-contained fixed-canvas HTML → html_export_readiness_skill (mandatory before every export AND every retry) → export_html_to_express. EXPORT TRANSPORT CORRECTED: the readiness skill's delivery section requires the FIRST available option, and because asset_initialize_file_upload is available on this connector, option 2 applies — upload the HTML with media_type text/html, curl PUT the block href, finalize, and pass the returned at.adobe.com presignedAssetUrl as export_html_to_express({url}). That host matches the importer's *.adobe.com allowlist and removes the payload ceiling. Inline html is permitted only for a document whose assembled payload is under 70 KB (realistically only the basis page, if that), because above that threshold the skill requires warning the user, which stalls an autonomous run. Stages 3–8 therefore carry the upload chain in their tool sets, and A22 asserts no export used inline html at or above 70 KB.

Every structural feature used is individually verified: multi-root documents in one call; mixed canvas sizes inside one document, which is what makes the 1080x1080 / 1080x1920 / 1200x628 / 1280x720 social set a single file; absolute mm units resolving at exactly 96 dpi, so 420x594mm gives 1587x2245 px; free-form absolute positioning of text, shapes and images; real editable text objects carrying family, pt size, colour and letter-spacing; real tables importing as table/table-row/table-cell with per-cell backgrounds and strokes, which is the deck's spec slide; inline SVG converting to native editable hz-shape paths, which is both the recovered mark and the comparison graphic; gradients, borders, radius, rotation and single box-shadows; auto-named slides from each root's heading. Photography is base64-inlined as data URIs on img elements — the one route verified to actually render — sized to on-canvas pixels within the stated per-document budget. No global canvasWidth/canvasHeight/slideSelector parameters are passed; every root self-describes.

VERIFICATION LOOP, WITH ITS LIMIT STATED ONCE. asset_search(entityScope CCAsset) → asset_get_presigned_urls → asset_inline_preview returns the rendered page back to the model, so author → export → look → fix → re-export is fully headless. But the rendition shows PAGE ONE ONLY: of 19 roots the agent can visually inspect 6. The spec therefore states the rule globally — root 1 of each document is verified visually, every other root is verified from the returned slides[].html structure, and each multi-root document must be ordered so its highest-risk canvas is root 1 — and A3 is re-pointed at base64 images decoded from the delivered source HTML rather than at renditions.

PRINT REALITY, STATED PLAINLY. download_design is not surfaced (re-checked live), so there is no file export out of Express in any format. mm units resolve at 96 dpi, so the A2 roots are 1587x2245 px layout masters, not press files. The client's own brief now says her marketing hire exports from Express, and the engagement requires a handover note stating the resolution reality and what would have to change for a genuinely press-ready A2. A13 is worded as a canvas-pixel assertion, not as a print-resolution claim.

DELIBERATELY ABSENT. No text-to-image, no generative fill, no AI object removal, no background-replace-by-prompt, no compositing, no upscaling, no OCR, no image_generative_expand, no per-artboard named export, no responsive or adaptive layout, no image placed into an Express template (replace_image is not surfaced), no download_design, no fill_text (non-deterministic, truncates, leaks label prefixes), no animate_design (returns four prose strings and no artifact), no create_firefly_board, no search_design, no variable QR, no InDesign or Illustrator path, and no video or audio tool of any kind — the entire async family is unretrievable headlessly and appears nowhere in this engagement. Batch sizes stay well under the ~20-file ceiling and the 10-image per-call cap. No step requires a human to click a widget, and the three mandatory-skill AskUserQuestion gates (template-vs-net-new, the regeneration gate, the visual-fidelity gate) are all pre-answered in the client's own words so a compliant agent never stalls.

element_reuse:
THREE elements are produced exactly once and then carried across the whole kit — six Express documents, nineteen roots.

(1) THE RECOVERED MARK. Traced once off the printed label in capture_06, cleaned once (leading full-canvas background path stripped, viewBox injected), then placed on the basis page in three colourways, on all three campaign directions, on the finished A2 poster, on all four social and paid canvases, on the three own-store product tiles and on all six deck slides — twenty placements of one geometry across eighteen of the nineteen roots. The nineteenth root, the marketplace primary tile, deliberately carries no mark because the channel forbids one; noticing that is part of the job. The three colourways are fill edits of that same geometry, not re-traces. A blob, an inverted plate, or a mark still carrying its opaque background rectangle breaks all twenty at once — and the background-rectangle defect is invisible on every light canvas and glaring on every dark one.

(2) THE TYPE KIT. One embed covering the entire system, pasted verbatim into all six source HTML files, with one shared numeric weight map derived from the style inventory. A single wrong slug, or a PostScript name written into font-family, ships the entire launch kit in a fallback sans, uniformly, across nineteen canvases.

(3) THE GRADED FRAMES. Six frames neutralised once in Stage 1 to one shared house look, then re-cropped per destination from the camera-scale source — A2, 1:1, 9:16, 1200x628, 1280x720 and 1200x1200. Re-cropping per destination is the correct move; rescaling one crop across six shapes clips the object at the vertical and loses the spec block at the ad strip. The same six frames also supply the deck's range slide and the product tiles, which is where a surviving session mismatch is most visible because corrected frames sit adjacent there.

A fourth reuse is the campaign line: written once, carried across the poster, all four social and paid units and the deck cover, with the buying occasion it targets named in the handover.

failure_gates: *** THIS ENTIRE FIELD IS GRADER-ONLY AND IS NEVER SHOWN TO THE AGENT. *** It is the scoring key, not a checklist to hand over. Every entry below states a wrong decision and its consequence; the agent receives only the client brief, brand_identity_additions minus design_implication, the deliverables list, catalogue.csv and the six captures.

SUBSTRATE-NAMED EXTRACTION FED TO THE TRACER. A prompt naming the label, the tag or the strap returns a plausible, successful, label-shaped mask; a prompt naming the ink by its colour and medium returns the mark. Score this on the DELIVERED GEOMETRY (A7/A9/A10), never on prompt strings — a substrate-named prompt used only to establish a crop bbox is legitimate and must not false-positive. The wrong choice yields a filled rectangle that then appears as a rectangle in twenty placements across six documents.

WRONG MASK POLARITY BEFORE TRACING. Tracing the raw selection returns a full-canvas dark plate with the mark knocked out of it — a negative that looks like a legitimate logo file in isolation and reads inverted the moment it lands on the dark poster and the dark deck cover. One inversion call is the entire difference and both paths report success.

SHIPPING THE TRACE UNHYGIENED. The tracer emits an opaque full-canvas rectangle as its first path and emits no viewBox at all. Left alone, the mark carries a hard box behind it on every dark canvas and refuses to scale across the six canvas sizes it has to survive.

USING BACKGROUND REMOVAL ON THE MARK. It detects one coherent subject; a disjoint printed lockup collapses to fragments of the lettering. The output looks like a partial logo, not like an error. The handover PNG must be rasterised locally from the cleaned SVG.

PLACING PHOTOGRAPHY BY URL. The connector's own image pipeline hands back real, fetchable image URLs on an Adobe host, and the mandatory readiness checklist explicitly says allowlisted hosts may be left as URLs — but in this environment they render as empty grey rectangles with a clean success reported. The CSS-background route with embedded data fails differently and equally silently. NOTE FOR SCORING: obeying the checklist here is not itself the failure; the hard gate is A15 (every declared photo slot actually carries image content), with A14 as a diagnostic.

UNMASKED RECOLOUR OF THE WEBBING. A whole-image colour operation on capture_02 and capture_06 drags the shovel handle, the traction board and the reference card with it, and the card can no longer read neutral — which invalidates the retained masters that are the sign-off artifact. image_apply_color_overlay has no mask parameter at all.

ONE GLOBAL CORRECTION, ONE SHARED PARAMETER SET, ONE PRESET, OR PER-FRAME AUTO-TONE. Six frames need six different corrections toward one shared neutral. Two group-wise corrections is the second-order version of the same mistake and must also fail: it looks fine in pairs and fractures the instant all six sit adjacent on the deck's range slide and in the product-tile row.

REACHING FOR PARAMETERS THAT DO NOT EXIST. There is no Kelvin temperature, no tint, no clarity, no whites and no blacks control. An agent that plans in those terms either stalls or logs values it never set.
MISSING THE OFF-LEVEL FRAME. Tone and crop operations cannot rotate; exactly one operation rectifies tilt. Skipping it ships a visibly canted product on whichever canvas that SKU lands.

LOSING THE REFERENCE CARD TO THE STRAIGHTEN. The rectifying operation crops back inside the rotated bounds by default. The card is set in from the corner precisely so this is survivable, but an agent that straightens after cropping tight, or that takes the card-bearing master from the unstraightened frame, ships an inconsistent pair.

THE REFLEXIVE NUMERIC WEIGHT. Numeric weights are non-standard per family, so the default body weight can ship Light where Regular was intended — uniformly, silently, across six documents, collapsing the editorial hierarchy the premium band depends on.

THE POSTSCRIPT NAME IN font-family. The name used to request the typeface never appears in the emitted CSS. Writing it into the stylesheet produces a silent fallback to a generic sans on every canvas, with no error anywhere in the chain. Any appearance of SourceSans3 or SourceSerif4 is unambiguously that fallback, because both are excluded as choosable faces.

ONE UNRESOLVABLE FONT NAME IN THE EMBED CALL. The call is all-or-nothing and case-sensitive, accepts only canonical PostScript names, and discards every valid font in the same call alongside the bad one.
UNSTYLED HEADINGS. Font weight is not inherited from HTML semantics; a heading with no explicit weight imports at Regular and the hierarchy flattens.

RIGHT- OR BOTTOM-ANCHORING A CONTENT-SIZED WRAPPER. A wrapper around the mark with no explicit width and height collapses to zero width, keeps its anchor, and throws the mark clipped off the canvas edge — while the export reports success.

GLOBAL CANVAS DIMENSIONS ON A MIXED-FORMAT SET. Passing canvas size as a tool parameter rather than declaring it per root collapses the deliberately mixed 1:1 / 9:16 / 1200x628 / 1280x720 set to a single size, destroying the entire point of the deliverable.
NAMING THE WRAPPER AS THE SLIDE UNIT. Pointing the slide selector at the container rather than the per-root class collapses a six-slide deck into one slide.

INLINE EXPORT AT SCALE. Every photograph must be base64-inlined, so any document carrying photography runs far past the 70 KB inline advisory. The correct route is to upload the HTML and export by URL. An agent that pushes a megabyte inline either stalls on a user warning or ships an unreliable import.

OBEYING THE PRE-FILLED EXPAND CHAIN. A severe cross-aspect crop returns a tradeoff carrying ready-made generative-expand arguments and a retry directive. Following it invokes the one generative tool this engagement bans, and the agent passes every other check while doing it.

TAKING THE FREE INTERPOLATION. The crop-and-resize operation will silently enlarge up to 2x and reports it only in a tradeoffs array that is easy to ignore, so a careless target size ships interpolated pixels into an A2 poster.

INVENTING A SPECIFICATION FIGURE. Every working load limit, breaking strength, material and weight is supplied. A number on a canvas that is not in catalogue.csv is a hard fail regardless of how plausible it is — this brand's whole positioning is published ratings.

PUTTING THE BUNDLE SAVING ON A CANVAS. The kit price is a fact; the saving against buying separately is internal and appears nowhere in the agent-facing brief. An agent that derives and displays it has invented discount grammar for a brand that has never discounted.

IMPULSE-BAND GRAMMAR AT A CONSIDERED-BAND PRICE. Cut-outs stacked on white across the owned surfaces, six SKUs crammed into one frame, price at display scale in a badge or burst, a saturated accent used as a field, one heavy condensed face doing every job. Each is defensible at $89 and each is wrong at $549 — and the client named two competitors whose look this reproduces.

OBEYING THE MARKETPLACE RULE EVERYWHERE, OR NOWHERE. The plain-ground, no-logo constraint applies to exactly one canvas. Applying it across the kit destroys the house look; ignoring it produces a listing image the channel rejects. The correct answer reconciles the two explicitly and says so in writing.

PROMISING A SEE-THROUGH APERTURE FROM BACKGROUND REMOVAL. On the marketplace primary the forged shackle's enclosed bow aperture stays filled with the captured plank and reads as a pale disc on the plain ground. The correct route is a material-named selection, inverted, filled to the ground colour so the aperture is filled too. This gate can now actually fire, because exactly one deliverable legitimately wants an isolated product.

PLANNING A LARGE HUE ROTATION TO A NAMED TARGET COLOUR. Safety-orange to muted clay is reachable as an adjacent-hue move plus desaturation plus darkening; an attempt at a big controlled rotation to a specific target produces mud across varied pixels.

VERIFYING ONLY WHAT THE PREVIEW SHOWS. The rendition returns page one only. An agent that checks the preview of a six-slide deck and stops has verified one sixth of the deliverable, and the same is true of the three- and four-root documents.
SUPPLYING THREE DIRECTIONS THAT ARE ONE LAYOUT RECOLOURED. Moving boxes around is not an argument. Three directions must differ in which element dominates the canvas and in which SKU carries it.

SUPPLYING FOUR SOCIAL UNITS THAT ARE ONE PICTURE IN FOUR SHAPES. Each unit has a different SKU, a different buying occasion and a different persuasion mechanic; an aspect-ratio permutation of one composition fails even if every canvas size is correct.

SHRINKING THE DECK TABLE ONTO THE PRODUCT SPEC TILE. The tile is read at thumbnail scale on a phone; the deck table is read across a meeting table and photographed. Same numbers, different information design.
hardness_rationale:
WHAT IS AUTO-GRADED AND WHAT IS NOT, STATED PLAINLY. The automatic suite proves hygiene, structure and factual fidelity: canvas pixels, root counts, distinct canvas sizes per root, resolved typeface families, explicit weights, catalogue values matching verbatim, mark geometry topology, no upscaling, no banned tool, no invented specification figure, no inline export at scale, six divergent parameter sets, region-confined recolour, and every declared photo slot actually carrying image content. It does NOT prove design quality. Every claim about whether this is good work rests on the sixteen human verifiers, and the human pass is budgeted as the real cost of grading this task, not as a garnish on the numbers.

THE FAILURE GATE IS A CHAIN OF WRONG DECISIONS, NONE OF WHICH ERRORS. The primary gate is mark recovery: naming the substrate rather than the ink returns a successful, plausible, label-shaped mask whose trace is a filled rectangle that then appears in twenty placements across six documents; getting the polarity wrong instead returns a knocked-out negative that looks like a real logo file and reads inverted only on the dark canvases; reaching for background removal returns a fragment of the lettering that looks like a partial logo rather than an error; and even the correct path emits an opaque background rectangle and no viewBox, so the mark ships with a hard box behind it on every dark surface and refuses to scale.

The second gate is photographic and is now genuinely six-way. The frames diverge inside each shooting session as well as across sessions, and the client no longer narrates a grouping, so sorting them into two piles is not an answer — the grader requires six distinct parameter sets with a written justification per frame, which defeats the two-global-corrections shortcut that the previous revision's verifier accepted. The parameter vocabulary is the tool's real one, so an agent planning in Kelvin, tint or clarity is planning in units that do not exist. The recolour must be region-confined or the reference card that is the entire sign-off mechanism stops reading neutral, and the only whole-image colour tool has no mask parameter at all.

The third gate is the layout surface, where every drop is silent: photography referenced rather than embedded becomes grey rectangles at HTTP 200; a PostScript name written into font-family falls back to a generic sans across six documents; the reflexive numeric weight ships Light on a family whose Regular is 500; one unresolvable name discards an entire font kit; a content-sized wrapper anchored right throws the mark clipped off the canvas; a globally-declared canvas size collapses the mixed-format social set; and the connector itself hands the agent a pre-filled generative-expand call it is not allowed to make.

HUMAN-HARD ELEMENTS THAT NO TOOL DOES. Cross-asset consistency across six differently-lit frames to a card-judged target with no readout and a downsampled preview. A type pairing the recommendation surface explicitly refuses to make, argued from a price band rather than adjectives. Three campaign directions whose premises the agent must invent and state, not select from a menu. A campaign line written from scratch and tied to one of three named buying occasions. Four social units that are four different arguments about four different SKUs at four different price points. An accent-colour decision the client has explicitly refused to make. A reconciliation between a house look built on full-frame quiet photography and one channel that forbids exactly that. Reuse rules — minimum size, clear space, colourway mapping — that the next freelancer will actually be handed. And holding nineteen canvases to a $549 considered-purchase grammar that the agent must DERIVE from price points, positioning, demographics and a named competitive set, because the design implication is grader-only and is never handed over. That derivation is checkable by the blind band-placement test with the price masked.

MEASURABILITY IS GRADER-SIDE AND HONEST ABOUT ITS TOLERANCES. The card-neutrality tolerance is set at a level an eyeball workflow on a downsampled preview can actually hit, with the real weight moved onto cross-frame agreement, which is what the client actually complained about. The held-space check measures non-photographic occupancy rather than bounding-box union, because a full-bleed photograph is the composition the brief wants. The ink-versus-substrate check is topological — path count and interior negative space — rather than an area-ratio heuristic that fails in both directions. The agent never reads a pixel; it reports the parameters it set, and any claimed measurement in the log is itself a failure.
one_line_ask: Take our six raw product frames, our attached spec sheet and the printed artwork on one of the straps, build the brand's visual system out of them, and deliver the whole launch kit — basis page, three key-visual directions and a defended pick, an A2 poster, a four-piece social and paid set, product-page and marketplace tiles, and the stockist deck — as six editable Adobe Express documents that all read as one brand.
options_required:
FIVE points where the agent must generate alternatives and defend a choice. No menu is supplied at any of them — the previous revision handed over the three direction premises and three ready-made headlines, which made two of these multiple-choice questions.

(1) THREE CAMPAIGN KEY-VISUAL DIRECTIONS at full A2 in a single document. No premises are given. The agent invents three genuinely different arguments about what sells this gear, states each one's premise in a sentence of its own, and must make them structurally divergent: no two roots may share the same dominant element (photograph / type block / recovered mark) or the same hero SKU, and the hero must be cropped at materially different scales across the three. Then a written pick argued from the $549 and $1,040 price points, the twice-a-decade purchase cycle and the two named look-alike competitors — never from adjectives.

(2) THE CAMPAIGN LINE. No copy exists. The agent writes three candidate lines pitched at genuinely different angles, names which of the three stated buying occasions each targets, picks one, and carries that one line across the poster, all four social and paid units and the deck cover.

(3) THE TYPE PAIRING. The recommendation surface returns roughly thirty on-brief candidates per role and explicitly refuses to pair, so heading-to-body is entirely the agent's art direction. It must shortlist, pair, and justify why the pairing reads at $549 rather than $89 — and it must not reproduce the heavy-condensed-everything look of the two competitors the client named.

(4) THE ACCENT COLOUR. The client has explicitly declined to decide between keeping the legacy green, killing it, or letting the current clay colourway carry the accent — and has said whatever is picked is what they are stuck with. The agent chooses, states the rule for how sparingly the accent is used, and argues the choice on the basis page.

(5) THE MARKETPLACE RECONCILIATION. The house look wants full-frame quiet photography; exactly one required canvas is governed by a channel rule demanding a plain uncluttered ground and forbidding any mark on it. The agent must decide how to hold the brand across that boundary — and must decide, given how product isolation actually behaves on a forged shackle with an enclosed aperture, whether isolation is even achievable for the SKU the client asked for and what it does instead if not. The decision goes in the handover note in writing.

In every case the alternatives must be genuinely divergent and the justification must reference price band, buying occasion or channel rules concretely.

stages.name: Stage 1 — Make six frames read as one deliberate set
stages.goal: AGENT-FACING GOAL: The client's six product frames do not belong together — the light is different in every one of them, one is off level, and two show last year's safety-orange webbing where the current run is a muted clay. Bring all six to one deliberate house look, judged against the reference card the client deliberately placed in each frame. Correct the webbing on the two affected frames so both read as the current colourway, leaving the shovel handle, the traction board and the reference card in those same frames exactly as they are. Hand back two distinct sets: six corrected masters with the reference card still in frame, for the client's sign-off, and six layout crops with the card excluded. Keep a written record of what you did to each frame and why it differs from the others.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-ONLY REFERENCE SOLUTION. Whether this is one correction, two, or six. All six frames diverge from each other — not just across two shooting sessions but within them — so a single global move, one shared preset, an auto-tone pass, or even two tidy group-wise corrections will leave the set visibly unmatched the moment the six sit adjacent on the deck's range slide and in the product-tile row. The agent must diagnose each frame independently against its own card and dial six different parameter sets toward one shared neutral, white point and black point. Second, the parameter vocabulary itself is a decision: the adjustment tool exposes a CIELAB triplet (tempA / tempB / tempLuminance, all three required together, positive tempA warming toward magenta and negative cooling toward green), exposure, gamma, exposureOffset, highlights, lights, darks, shadows, vibrance, saturation and an HSL triple — there is no Kelvin, no tint, no clarity, no whites and no blacks, so an agent planning in those terms is planning in units it cannot set. Third, the webbing recolour must be region-confined; the only whole-image colour tool has no mask parameter at all, and an unmasked move drags the card. The move itself is adjacent-hue plus strong desaturation plus a lightness reduction, not a rotation to a named target hex, which produces mud. Fourth, exactly one frame is off level and no tone or crop operation rotates, so the agent must notice by eye and reach for the one rectifying operation — and because that operation crops back inside the rotated bounds by default, the card-bearing master for that frame must be taken after straightening.

Choose the typefaces and pair them yourself, and argue the pairing from what this gear costs and who buys it rather than from adjectives. Decide the accent-colour question the client has explicitly left open — legacy green, no green, or the clay of the current webbing — and argue that too. Show the recovered mark in its three colourways, and write the rules that stop the next person wrecking it: minimum reproduction size in mm for print and px for screen, clear space as a fraction of the mark, which colourway belongs on which kind of surface, and a short do-not list. The type must arrive as live editable text in the real licensed faces, not as a picture of type.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-ONLY REFERENCE SOLUTION. The pairing. The recommendation surface returns roughly thirty on-brief candidates per role and explicitly refuses to pair, so heading-to-body is entirely the agent's art direction and must be argued from the price band. A signage-heritage or editorial display face paired with a neutral text face reads considered; the heavy-condensed-slab-everything answer reads like the two competitors the client named and like an $89 kit. SourceSans3 and SourceSerif4 are excluded as choosable faces, so any appearance of either is unambiguously the fallback. stages.name: Stage 4 — Three campaign directions and a defended pick
stages.goal: AGENT-FACING GOAL: Three genuinely different arguments for the campaign key visual, at full A2, delivered as one document the client can flip through. Not one layout in three colours — three different claims about what actually sells this gear, each of which has to remain defensible at $549 a pair. traps: *** GRADER-ONLY. NEVER SHOWN TO THE AGENT. ***

The connector's own image pipeline returns genuine, fetchable image URLs on an Adobe host, and the mandatory readiness checklist explicitly tells the agent that allowlisted Adobe hosts may be left as URLs because the importer resolves them natively. In this environment they do not resolve — they render as empty grey boxes with no warning anywhere in the chain. Obeying the documentation is the trap. Scoring must therefore gate on the rendered/structural result, not on whether the agent disobeyed Adobe's checklist.

Every silent drop returns HTTP success: missing images, blurred grounds, blend modes, stroked and outlined display type, text shadows, multi-column body copy, backdrop filters, underlines, outlines, and every drop-shadow layer after the first. A rugged-brand design instinct reaches straight for blend modes and outlined type, and those elements simply are not in the delivered file.

The crop tool's default clipping behaviour hands the agent a pre-filled generative-expand call and a retry directive on any severe cross-aspect crop — actively instructing it to use the one generative tool the engagement bans, with no indication that this is out of bounds.
Crop-and-resize will silently interpolate up to 2x and reports it only inside a tradeoffs array; the operation otherwise looks like a clean downscale.

Automatic background removal succeeds and looks correct on a light ground while leaving every enclosed aperture filled; on the marketplace tile the defect appears only once the shackle sits on the plain ground.
Background removal is also the intuitive tool for the logo, and on a disjoint printed lockup it returns a fragment of the lettering that reads as a partial logo rather than as a failure.
The straightening operation crops back inside the rotated bounds by default, so a corner-placed reference element can be clipped away by the very operation meant to fix the frame.

The adjustment tool's parameter list does not contain the controls a photographer would reach for by name — no Kelvin temperature, no tint, no clarity, no whites, no blacks — and the stale internal documentation says otherwise.

A tempting shortcut exists for the social set — a template search plus a text-fill call — and it is a dead end: the fill operation is non-deterministic across identical calls, truncates content, and leaks field labels onto the canvas as literal text.
A second tempting shortcut exists for the deck — an animation call — and it produces no artifact at all, only four descriptive strings.

The type-embed request is all-or-nothing and case-sensitive: it accepts only canonical PostScript names, rejects family names outright, and one unresolvable entry discards the entire kit including every valid font in the same call.

The PostScript name never appears in the emitted CSS, and the two faces the importer falls back to are themselves legitimate, choosable Adobe fonts — so a fallback and a deliberate choice are indistinguishable unless those two faces are excluded up front.
The documented fallback for finding a close match to a known typeface is broken — similarity lookup on a face alone returns unrelated categories entirely.

Every photograph must be embedded rather than linked, so payload adds up fast; the readiness skill's inline route requires warning the user above 70 KB, which stalls an autonomous run, while the correct route (upload the HTML, export by URL) is one option further down a list the agent has to read carefully.
The rendition preview shows root 1 only, so of nineteen roots the agent can visually confirm six. An agent that checks previews and stops has verified a third of the kit at best.

Tool responses in the template family carry a large embedded instruction block telling the agent to stop and ask the user to pick from a gallery; obeying it stalls an autonomous run, and it is not enforced anywhere server-side.
The font family's response payloads carry roughly four kilobytes of prose style-guide instructions per call — instructional text returned as tool output, to be treated as data, not as direction.
The client explicitly declines to make the accent-colour decision, which is an invitation to leave it unmade. Nineteen canvases depend on it.
The marketplace rule is stated as an external constraint the client dislikes, which invites the agent either to apply it everywhere for consistency or to quietly ignore it. Both are wrong.
