verifiers_human.text: The four social and paid units are four different arguments about four different products at four different price points, each aimed at an identifiable buying occasion — not one composition in four shapes.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer views the four canvases and names, for each, the SKU, the occasion and the persuasion mechanic; assert four distinct answers.

verifiers_human.text: The campaign line is genuinely written for this brand, is carried consistently across poster, all four social units and the deck cover, and the three candidates offered were meaningfully different from each other rather than three phrasings of one idea.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer reads the three candidates and traces the pick across six surfaces.

verifiers_human.text: The marketplace primary would pass the channel's rules and still be recognisably from this brand's world — and the reconciliation the freelancer wrote is a real argument, not an apology. The shackle's bow reads clean through, with no ghost of the plank inside it.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer inspects the tile at full size against the stated channel rules and reads the reconciliation paragraph.

verifiers_human.text: The deck would survive a real buyer meeting: it opens with a claim, the range slide is legible, the spec table is the kind of thing a buyer photographs, and the price ladder closes without apologising or discounting.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer runs the six slides as if presenting.

verifiers_human.text: Nothing in the kit reads as discount retail: no urgency, no badge, no crowding, no shouting, and the prices sit comfortably alongside the specifications.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer scans all nineteen canvases for retail-promotional grammar.

verifiers_human.text: The mark, the palette, the accent decision and the type read as one system across all nineteen roots — a reviewer shown any single canvas in isolation would assign it to this brand (excepting the marketplace primary, which is judged only on channel compliance and product quality).
verifiers_human.how: Single-canvas attribution test across the six documents.

verifiers_human.text: Held space on the poster is doing work rather than being empty by accident — the poster feels composed, not sparse.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer judgement at size.

verifiers_human.text: The basis page would actually serve the next freelancer: the reuse rules are specific enough to follow, the accent decision is owned and argued, and a stranger could place the mark correctly on a new surface without asking anyone.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer is handed only the basis page and asked to place the mark on an unseen dark canvas and on an unseen light one, and to say what size is too small.

verifiers_human.text: A novice's version would be visibly worse: the reviewer can point to at least three decisions in the delivered kit that a competent freelancer made and a naive one would not have.
verifiers_human.how: Reviewer names the decisions unprompted.

why_not_a_vlm_one_shot:
A vision-language model can describe every one of these deliverables and can generate a picture that resembles one. It cannot produce any of them. Four reasons, and they compound.

First, the artifacts are not images. The client asked for editable Adobe Express documents their marketing hire can open and change a price in — six of them, nineteen artboards, one of which is a six-slide deck containing a live table with per-cell structure that a buyer will update next quarter, and one of which is a poster at A2 dimensions with the recovered company mark sitting in it as editable vector paths. A one-shot model returns a flat raster. It cannot return a native document with live text in a licensed typeface, a real table, and editable vector geometry, and it cannot return six of them sharing one font embed and one weight map.

Second, the inputs are real and the model cannot make them up. Six actual camera frames exist, each lit differently, with a physical reference card placed in each specifically so someone could reconcile them. A generative model does not correct those frames — it invents different ones, and the client's product photography is replaced by pictures of gear that does not exist. Likewise the company's only surviving artwork is a print on a physical label; recovering it means tracing that specific ink at ink level, fixing the polarity, and cleaning three defects the tracer introduces. A generative model draws a plausible logo instead, which is not the client's logo, which is the entire problem the client hired someone to solve. And every load rating, breaking strength, material and weight is a supplied fact for load-rated recovery gear; a model that invents one has invented a safety claim.

Third, the failure modes are invisible in the model's own output. Every silent drop in this pipeline returns success. A photograph referenced rather than embedded becomes an empty grey rectangle and reports HTTP 200 — and the connector's own mandatory checklist tells the agent that referencing it is fine. A trace shipped with its background path intact looks perfect on every light canvas and carries a hard box on every dark one. A typeface requested by the wrong name string falls back to a generic sans across six documents with no error anywhere, and the two faces it falls back to are themselves real fonts. A default numeric weight ships Light where Regular was meant. A canvas size passed as a parameter rather than declared per root collapses a deliberately mixed four-format social set into one shape. Automatic isolation leaves the space inside a shackle bow filled with the plank behind it. None of these produce an error, a warning, or a visibly broken tool response. Catching them requires the agent to author, export, look at what it actually produced, recognise which of a dozen look-alike defects it is seeing, and go back and fix the cause — a closed loop over real artifacts, run six times, on a surface where only the first artboard of each document can be looked at and the rest must be verified structurally.

Fourth, and most decisive: most of this job is not a picture at all. It is deciding that six frames need six different corrections rather than one or two, in a parameter vocabulary that does not contain the controls a photographer would name. Deciding that the recolour must be region-confined or the reference card stops being a reference. Pairing a display face to a text face when the recommendation surface explicitly refuses to pair. Making an accent-colour decision the client has flatly declined to make. Writing a campaign line from nothing and tying it to one of three named buying occasions. Inventing three campaign arguments rather than picking from a menu, and then defending one. Giving four social units four different products, four occasions and four persuasion mechanics instead of four crops. Reconciling a house look built on quiet full-frame photography against one channel that forbids exactly that and forbids the logo too. Writing reuse rules — minimum size, clear space, colourway mapping — that a stranger will have to follow. And deriving, from six price points, a positioning line, a demographic and a named competitive set, an entire visual grammar for $549 rather than $89 — and holding it across nineteen canvases — when nobody hands that grammar over. That is a week of a competent freelancer's judgement, expressed as a dependent chain where an early wrong decision does not error; it quietly ruins the thing three stages later.

engagement_title: Corner-unit launch kit — El Vecino Cocina, second location
one_line_ask: Take a neighbourhood taqueria's six surviving image files, a 2019 brand sheet PDF, the printer's PDF of last year's table tent and one spreadsheet, and build the whole launch kit for their second unit — recovered brand elements, a chosen art direction, street and in-store pieces, a mixed-format social set, paid units, delivery-listing dish images, a partner deck with real numbers, and a variable-data tent-card print run — all sharing one mark, one type system, one price convention and one set of trading facts.

brand_identity_additions.price_range: Tacos $3.75 each, three for $10.50. The weekday 'Comida Corrida' lunch plate is $12.50 flat and includes rice, beans and an agua fresca. Aguas frescas $3. Kids plate $6.50. Nothing on the à la carte board is above $18. The one exception is the Family Platter at $34, which is a shared item sold off the board for three-to-four people — it is not an à la carte dish and is never quoted as a per-person price. Average lunch ticket $14.20; average dinner ticket $21.40. No service charge, cash and card, no minimum.
brand_identity_additions.positioning: The everyday corner kitchen — not a destination, not a concept. Second-generation family operation, open since 2019, counter service with eight tables and a takeout window. Competes on speed, portion size and being trusted; explicitly not competing on chef-driven novelty. The promise is 'you can afford to eat here twice a week and you will.'
brand_identity_additions.demographics: Weekday 11:30–2:00 is trades, warehouse and hospital shift workers, transit and city crews, plus office staff from the two low-rise blocks up the avenue — median household income around $52,000, ticket paid in under four minutes, back at work in thirty-five. Evenings and weekends skew families with kids under twelve and 20s–30s renters from the surrounding blocks. Roughly 60% of the lunch crowd orders in Spanish first; almost all of them also read English. Buying occasion is habitual, not aspirational: a fast weekday plate, a Friday family takeout order, a Sunday sit-down after church league games. Sidewalk decisions are made in under five seconds, at distance, often while crossing a four-lane avenue; in-store decisions are made standing in a queue three to five metres from the wall, in about ninety seconds, from the full twelve-dish board.
brand_identity_additions.competitive_set: Two other taquerias within six blocks at the same price band, a fried-chicken counter, a pho counter, and three national fast-food units on the same avenue whose signage is enormous, saturated and price-forward. The client is not competing with the wine-bar block eleven minutes north.
brand_identity_additions.design_implication: [GRADER-ONLY — THIS FIELD IS THE WITHHELD REFERENCE KEY AND MUST NOT BE SHOWN TO THE AGENT. It is the answer the agent is supposed to derive from price_range + demographics + competitive_set alone.] The price band is the design brief. At $3.75 a taco and $12.50 for a full lunch plate, price is the headline, not a footnote — it has to be readable at distance, in the heading face, at display scale, and the offer must resolve before the brand name does. The palette runs saturated and warm because it has to hold its own against fast-food signage on the same street, not recede from it. The food grade must be bright, open-shadowed and appetite-forward — a plate that looks like a generous $12.50, photographed as if under the restaurant's own lights at noon. Copy sits in plain bilingual register: 'Plato del día, $12.50 / Lunch plate, $12.50 — out in ten minutes', never 'thoughtfully composed'. Language is a per-surface decision, not a global one: at 320×50 there is no room for two languages and the correct call is Spanish-first on the surfaces read by the lunch queue and the sidewalk, English-secondary where a second line fits, and one language only where it does not — with the reasoning stated. The recovered mark is used large and sign-like, the way a painted window or an awning uses it. THE COUNTERFACTUAL, and this is the load-bearing part: if this brand sat at $28 a plate with a $95 tasting menu, every one of those decisions inverts — prices would be suppressed or omitted entirely from the poster, type would shrink and open up with wide margins and generous negative space, the palette would drop to low chroma, the grade would go low-key, moody and under-lit with closed shadows, the mark would be reduced to a small quiet monogram, and the copy would move to an evocative register. An agent that reaches for the default 'premium restaurant' look — dark, desaturated, minimal, price in 8pt at the bottom — has produced a technically clean deliverable for the wrong business, and it is visible on sight. Grading note: score whether the agent DERIVED this from the numbers and the audience, not whether these words appear.

client_brief:
Hi — Marisol here, we spoke last week. I'll try to give you everything at once because I'm terrible at answering email during service.

Quick background. We're El Vecino Cocina. My mother and I opened in 2019 in a converted laundromat, counter service, eight tables and a takeout window. In seven weeks we take the keys on a second unit, a corner spot on the avenue where the old hardware store was — glass on two sides, a lot of foot traffic, and a bus stop directly outside. That corner is the whole reason we signed. It also means we are now standing on the same street as three national chains with signage the size of a garage door.

Who eats with us: at lunch it's trades, warehouse crews, hospital shift staff, transit and city guys, and the office people from the two low-rise blocks up the avenue. They have about thirty-five minutes total, door to door, and most of them order in Spanish. Evenings and weekends it's families with young kids and the renters from our blocks. Our tacos are $3.75, three for $10.50. The Comida Corrida lunch plate is $12.50 and that includes rice, beans and an agua fresca. Aguas frescas are $3, kids plate $6.50, nothing on the board goes over $18, and the Family Platter is $34 but that's a share plate for three or four people, not one person's dinner. Average lunch ticket is $14.20. I'm telling you the numbers because I want them to be the point, not something you tuck into a corner. Somebody crossing four lanes of traffic should know what it costs before they know what we're called. We are not the wine-bar block eleven minutes north and I don't want to look like we're pretending to be.

The details you'll need on everything: the new unit is 1140 Alameda Avenue, on the corner of Alameda and 12th. We open Tuesday 14 October. Hours are 11:00 to 21:00 Tuesday to Saturday, 11:00 to 17:00 Sunday, closed Monday — kitchen stops thirty minutes before close. Phone is (555) 0142. Our delivery listing handle and our social handle are both elvecinococina. We don't have a website and I'm not paying for one this year, so anything that needs a click should send people to the delivery listing.

Now the awkward part. The designer who did our original identity in 2019 stopped answering in 2021 and we do not have any of the original files. What I can send you is what actually survives on my laptop and my phone.

Six pictures. Four of them are food — our neighbour's daughter shot some of them for us last spring on a real camera and I took at least one myself on my phone, and honestly they don't all look like they came from the same restaurant, which drives me a little crazy. Those four are the only dishes we have pictures of. The other twelve on the menu have never been photographed and there is no time to fix that before we open. The last two pictures both have our logo in them somehow. I don't know which of those two is the better starting point — you'll have to look at them and tell me. Whatever you can get out of them, I need it to be one thing we can use everywhere: on the awning eventually, on the window, and on everything you're making now. It has to hold up on a dark background as well as a light one.

A one-page PDF the old designer sent us with our colours and the name of the typeface he used — he wrote it as Calzada Grotesk. I have no idea if that's still a thing you can get, or if it's even right for us now. Use your judgement — I'd rather you tell me what you think we should be, and show me a couple of directions, than have you match a five-year-old sheet nobody remembers.

One spreadsheet. First tab is the full menu — twelve dishes, names in Spanish and English, prices, allergen notes, and which station makes them; my son typed it up. Second tab is our trading details, the ones I just gave you, so you have them written down. Third tab is covers by daypart and the money side — rent on the new unit, what the fit-out is costing us, average ticket by daypart, and what we're trying to raise.

A PDF from our printer of the little table tent cards we used last year. That's the only form it exists in; the printer never gave us anything else. We want to reprint them for the new unit. The printer just needs a press-ready file from us and he'll do the rest.

What I need from you by the opening:

A poster for the corner window at A3, and artwork for the two bus shelters we've booked — the media company sent a spec sheet, the printed face is 1185 by 1750 millimetres and they want it supplied at a scale with the scale marked on it. It has to sell the $12.50 lunch plate hard, and it has to work from the far side of the avenue.

Something for inside. We have a big blank wall behind the counter and nothing on it — the queue stands there reading nothing for a minute and a half. I want a proper menu board with all twelve dishes and the prices on it, and something on the two glass frontages and the door so the corner reads as ours from outside.

A social set. One square for the feed, one vertical for stories, one wide one. Same idea across all three, not three different ideas. And please write me the captions and tell me what to post and when — I'm running service, I'm not going to invent a launch campaign between tickets.

Ads for the local news site — they sell a small box, a long banner and the little strip that shows on phones — plus a paid square for social. Those need to work with almost no room, and the click should go to our delivery listing.

Dish images for our delivery listing. The platform sent us their rules and they're strict: no text on the picture, no logos, no watermarks, no price, just the food on a clean background. They also sell a separate promo tile inside the app where you ARE allowed to put an offer on it, and I want one of those too.

A short deck for the landlord and for my uncle, who is putting money in. Six or seven slides. It needs our lunch-hour numbers in it as an actual table and one simple chart of covers by daypart, and my uncle will ask what the rent is, when we break even and how much I'm asking him for — those numbers are all on the third tab. This is the one that has to look like a real business, not a family project.

And the tent cards, press-ready.

Three more things. First: before you build any of it, show me a couple of genuinely different directions and tell me which one you'd pick and why, in terms of my customers and my prices, not in terms of design words. And show them to me on something real — put each one on a small version of the actual poster so I can see what I'd be walking past, not just squares of colour. I want to be able to disagree with you knowingly. Second: whatever you pull out of that logo, use the same one everywhere. Last time we ended up with four slightly different versions floating around and my mother noticed before anyone else did. Third: send everything to me as editable Adobe Express documents plus whatever source files you build them from, shared to my email so my son can open them and change a price himself — and please build these from scratch for us rather than off a stock template, because the whole point is that the plate in the picture is the plate you actually get.

Budget: I have about $6,000 and a hard opening date. Tell me honestly what I need for opening day and what can wait until month two, and what I should spend the next money on. If something on my list isn't worth doing at my size, say so.

stages.name: S1 — Intake, look hard, and set the photographic direction
stages.goal: Get every client input into the working environment, look at each one before deciding what it is, and land the food photography on a single deliberate look that suits this price band and this audience — including the frames that were not shot under the same conditions as the others.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Four decisions, none stated in the agent-facing brief. (1) What look does a $12.50-lunch-plate, shift-worker, sidewalk-decision business actually need — bright, open-shadow, appetite-forward, surviving at small size and speed, or the low-key moody grade that is every model's reflex for 'restaurant photography'? The second is wrong here and the wrongness is visible on sight, and it propagates into every photographic surface in the kit. (2) Three of the four food frames carry a small grey reference card in the corner; the agent must notice it exists and use it as the neutrality anchor rather than trusting an automatic tone pass. (3) The frames were shot under different light — two under warm interior lamps in the evening, one by a window at midday, one on a phone under mixed fluorescent. Converging them requires different corrections per frame, judged by eye; identical parameters across all four, or an independent auto pass on each, leaves plates that visibly belong to different restaurants, which is the complaint the client already voiced. (4) One frame is a phone capture at roughly 1600×1200 with no reference card. The agent must work out, unprompted, that this frame cannot carry a print-scale hero or a full-bleed 300-density card without enlargement, must match it by eye without a card, and must decide where it can legitimately be used — or exclude it and say so. One frame is also visibly tilted and needs rectifying before any tonal work, which nothing tells the agent.
subtasks: Bring every supplied file into the working environment and look at each one before deciding what it is or what it needs.
Decide, from the price band and the lunch-hour audience, what the food should look like, and state that decision before applying it.
Bring all four food frames onto one shared, deliberate look so they read as one kitchen under one set of lights, correcting each frame as much or as little as it individually needs.
Retain, per frame, a full-frame corrected master exactly as corrected, before any crop is taken from it.
Produce, from those masters, the crops every later piece needs at the sizes those pieces need, without ever enlarging beyond what the source supports.
Record, per frame, the settings you actually applied and one line on why that frame needed different numbers from the others.
State which frames are fit for which surfaces, and name any frame you decided not to use on a given surface and why.
stages.feeds_into: S2 (every cutout is cut from these masters, so a bad grade is baked into the tiles and the printed cards), S4, S5, S6, S7.

stages.name: S2 — Recover the brand elements once, and build the reuse library
stages.goal: Turn the two logo-bearing files into one clean, placeable, scalable mark plus a small library of derived elements that every later piece draws from — recovered once, reused everywhere.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] The triage is genuinely ambiguous from the outside: two same-kind raster files, neutrally named, both containing the mark. One is a small flat web-era export with a baked-in soft shadow and resampling artifacts — the obvious-looking source, which yields a mushy, shadow-contaminated trace that cannot go to awning scale. The other is a phone photograph of hand-painted door glass with a ring of lettering around the emblem — harder, and the only source that supports a clean scalable mark. They do not take the same treatment. The naive route on the photographed one — asking for 'the logo on the door' and then knocking out its background — returns a door-panel-shaped blob or a solid opaque disc with the ring's negative space filled; both report success. A stroke-accurate recovery requires naming what the ink itself looks like rather than what it sits on, and requires deciding isolation polarity before tracing. Then two defects the tools never report: the traced result arrives with an opaque full-canvas plate behind it and no intrinsic scaling box, and the client asked by name for a mark that holds on a dark ground and works on an awning. The agent must notice both itself. Finally the reversed version: it is not reachable by hue adjustment on a raster — it comes from editing the fill values on the cleaned vector, so that the placed mark stays the same geometry everywhere. Ordering matters on the cutouts too: cutting a camera-scale master and cropping afterwards can force an enlargement at delivery size, so the reduction has to happen first.
subtasks: Decide which of the two logo-bearing files can actually yield a usable mark, and say what fails in the other — show them side by side on a dark ground so the client can see the difference you are describing.

Deliver one mark that stays sharp when it is used at awning size, reads correctly on a dark ground with its enclosed shapes reading as holes, and can be placed on any surface in the kit without a box around it.
Deliver a second, colour-faithful version of the same mark for use on a light field, preserving the painted colours.
Deliver exactly two shipping states of that mark — the positive for light grounds and the reversed for dark grounds — built so that the shape is identical in both and only the colour differs.
Prepare the dishes as reusable elements: cleanly separated from their backgrounds, and also as versions sitting on a flat ground, at the sizes the later pieces need.
Produce one reusable surface texture derived from the client's own material, sized for the pieces it will sit behind.
Name every element in the library and state which element is the correct one for which surface.
stages.feeds_into: S3 (recovered colours inform the palette), S4, S5, S6, S7 (the dish elements are bound per row into the printed cards, so a bad separation ships to press).

stages.name: S3 — Type, palette, language rule, and three directions the client can choose between
stages.goal: Establish a real, licensed, buildable type system and colour palette, decide how the two languages behave surface by surface, present three genuinely different directions on something the client can judge, and commit to one with a written rationale grounded in her prices and her customers.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Four decisions. (1) Pairing: nothing in the environment will pair a display face with a text face and the recommendation surface explicitly refuses to, so the heading/text pairing is entirely the agent's art direction. (2) Weights: style names and numeric weights do not correspond consistently across families, so the reflexive regular weight can silently resolve to Light on a poster whose only job is legibility across four lanes. (3) The brand sheet names a face that does not exist in the library; a single embed request containing that name fails wholesale and discards every valid face with it, so names must be laundered before any embed is built, and the substitution is an art-direction decision, not a lookup. (4) Language: the demographics say roughly 60% of the lunch crowd orders in Spanish first, but no deliverable says which language leads on which surface. At 320×50 both will not fit. The agent must set an explicit per-surface rule and defend it. Then the directions themselves must be three real alternatives — different photographic intent, different palette logic, different typographic voice — not one layout in three colourways, and each must be shown on a small full composition of the actual poster because that is what the client asked to judge. The pick must be argued in her terms: price, decision distance, thirty-five-minute lunch, the chain signage on the same avenue. A direction that would be right at $28 a plate is wrong at $12.50 and the agent has to say why.
subtasks: Read what the 2019 brand sheet actually states and decide how much of it survives, including whether its named typeface is still obtainable and what you would use instead if it is not.
Choose a heading face that holds at sign scale across a four-lane avenue and a text face that keeps a $3.75 price line legible small, and get every weight you use right.
Set up the type so it renders in the real licensed faces in every piece you build, and record the exact reference each face must be written with.
Define the palette: a primary, a secondary, a dark ground, a light ground, and one accent reserved for price, working in both directions.
Decide, surface by surface, which language leads, which is secondary, and where only one fits — and be ready to defend the rule.

Present three genuinely different directions in one document, one per slide, each carrying the mark, the type hierarchy, the palette with the price accent called out, a food frame treated that direction's way, and a small full composition of the corner-window poster in that direction.
Look at what you exported and correct it before you present it.

Write the recommendation: which direction, why, in the client's terms — her prices, her lunch hour, how far away the decision gets made, what is on the same street — and what the other two would have been right for.
stages.feeds_into: S4, S5, S6, S7 — every later piece is built on the committed direction, so a direction chosen against the price band propagates into eleven artifacts.

stages.name: S4 — The street: corner-window poster and bus-shelter face
stages.goal: Produce the two outdoor pieces — an A3 corner-window poster and the booked bus-shelter face at its true trim, supplied at a marked scale — both selling the $12.50 lunch plate to someone at distance.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Three decisions. (1) Hierarchy: the client said the cost must resolve before the name, at distance, so the offer and the number outrank the mark and the brand line — the opposite of the instinctive layout. Two poster layouts must genuinely differ in how they solve that, and one must be chosen with a stated account of what the loser did worse. (2) The shelter face is not a scaled-up A3. It is a different aspect (roughly 2:3 against A3's 1:1.41), read from a bus queue at three metres and from across the avenue, and it must be supplied at a marked reduction with the true trim stated — recomposing it rather than rescaling the poster is the professional move and the difference is visible. (3) How the photography gets into the layout at all: the layout route will accept a photograph referenced by address, export successfully, report success, and render an empty box — including addresses on the platform's own hosts. Only looking at the rendered result reveals it. Attached to that: the embedded photograph is fixed at its placed pixel box, so a hero embedded at its CSS size prints soft at A3 and unusable at shelter scale; the agent must embed at a multiple and must disclose the effective resolution and how the printer gets a file, because no flat export exists on this route. Two further silent hazards: several effects an agent naturally reaches for on a food poster are discarded on import, and outlined display type with a transparent fill vanishes entirely; and the payload gets large fast once real photography is embedded, which has a documented route around it that the agent must find.
subtasks: Author two different corner-window poster layouts at true A3 physical dimensions using the committed direction, the recovered mark and the graded hero.
Get the photography into the layouts in a form that actually renders, and confirm by looking that it rendered rather than assuming it did.
Choose one layout and state what the rejected one did worse against the test of being read from the far side of the avenue.
Author the bus-shelter face at the media owner's true trim, supplied at a marked scale, composed for its own shape and its own viewing distance rather than rescaled from the poster.
State the effective resolution of every printed piece and exactly what the client's printer or media owner will need from her to produce it.
Verify what you exported by looking at it, correct it, and export again; say plainly which parts you were able to see and which you could not.
stages.feeds_into: S5 and S6 reuse the committed hierarchy and price treatment; S8.

stages.name: S5 — In-store: menu board and window/door graphics
stages.goal: Produce the pieces that work on the site itself — a counter menu board carrying all twelve dishes and the whole price architecture, and graphics for the two glass frontages and the door.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] The menu board is the only surface where the full price architecture has to resolve as a system rather than as one hero number: $3.75 each and three for $10.50 are the same offer stated two ways, the $12.50 plate is an inclusive price that has to say what it includes, the $34 platter is a share item that must not read as one person's dinner, and $3 aguas and a $6.50 kids plate have to sit in the hierarchy without competing. It is read from three to five metres by someone with ninety seconds, so the dish list has to be a real structured table with live text the client's son can edit, at a size that holds at queue distance — and the bilingual rule set in S3 has to survive twelve rows without doubling the board's height. The window and door graphics are a different problem: tall narrow apertures, seen from outside against interior light, where the mark is used at sign scale and almost nothing else survives. Both are large physical formats supplied at a marked scale, and both must state their trim.
subtasks: Author a counter menu board at a true physical size for the wall behind the counter, supplied at a marked scale with its trim stated, carrying all twelve dishes with prices as a genuine structured list the client's son can edit.

Make the whole price architecture readable as a system at queue distance, including how the taco single and three-for price relate, what the lunch plate includes, and that the family platter is a share item.
Author graphics for the two glass frontages and the door at their own proportions, carrying the mark at sign scale and the lunch offer.
Apply the language rule you set, and say what you did on the board where twelve rows made a second language expensive.
Verify what you exported by looking at it, correct it, and say which parts you could not see.
stages.feeds_into: S8 (consistency sweep, phasing — the in-store pieces are the ones that most obviously ship or wait).

stages.name: S6 — Social set, paid units, and the delivery-listing images
stages.goal: Produce the channel pieces: a three-format social set that reads as one idea, four paid units that survive near-zero room, three delivery-listing dish images that obey the platform's rules, and one in-app promo tile that does not have to.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Three different compression problems plus a channel-rules problem. (1) The social set must be one document carrying three different canvas sizes, and how the document declares those sizes determines whether the client gets a three-format set or three copies of one size; the aspect extremes are far enough apart that a scaled square is obvious in the vertical. (2) The paid units run to a 320×50 strip where only the number and the offer survive — the agent must decide what it drops at each size and say so, and at this price band the number survives before the mark does. (3) The listing images are governed by the platform's rules the client quoted: no text, no logo, no price. That removes every typographic crutch, so brand recognition has to be carried by ground, colour and the cut of the food alone — and the images have to be handed over as ordinary flat files the client can upload, which the layout route cannot produce, so they must be produced by the imaging route instead. Whether each dish reads better cleanly separated on a built ground or knocked onto a flat colour depends on how that dish actually separated in S2, and one of them will not separate cleanly. The promo tile is the only place the price is allowed, and it is not a listing image, so it goes down the layout route. There is also a standing temptation to start from a ready-made template for 'a few social posts' — that route cannot accept the client's own photography at all, which is the one thing she said the business is built on.
subtasks: Author the three social canvases as one document, each at its own size, sharing one idea, one message, one mark, one type system and one palette — composed for each shape rather than scaled.
Author the four paid units at the sizes the news site sells plus the paid social square, and state for each what you dropped and why, keeping the offer legible at the smallest.
Make sure every paid unit points to the destination the client named.

Produce the three delivery-listing dish images as ordinary flat image files the client can upload directly, obeying the platform's rules exactly, deciding per dish how it is best presented based on how it actually separated.
Produce the in-app promo tile, where the offer is allowed, in the committed direction.
Verify everything you exported by looking at it, correct it, and say which parts you could not see.
stages.feeds_into: S7 (the dish elements chosen here are the same ones bound into the printed cards), S8.

stages.name: S7 — The partner deck
stages.goal: Produce a six-to-seven slide deck for the landlord and the investor that reads as a real business case — with the lunch-hour numbers as a genuine table, covers by daypart as an editable chart, and the money question answered.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] This is the one piece whose audience is not a customer, so the register must shift toward a business reader without abandoning the identity. The harder part is that the deck has to do arithmetic the client's price band drives and that no input states directly: covers by daypart against average ticket by daypart gives revenue, revenue against rent plus operating cost gives a break-even covers-per-day figure, and the amount being raised has to appear as a number with a use for it. An agent that renders the supplied figures without computing the break-even has produced a brand deck with a chart in it. The table has to be a real structured table with per-cell text, and the chart has to be genuine editable artwork, not a picture of a chart, because the client's son is expected to change a number in it later.
subtasks: Author a six-to-seven slide deck: cover, the offer, the corner and its traffic, the lunch-hour numbers, covers by daypart, the room, and the ask.
Build the numbers as a genuine structured table and the daypart figures as a chart that stays editable by a non-designer — not a picture of one.
Work the money question out from the figures the client supplied and put the answer on a slide: what it costs to run, what it takes to break even, what is being asked for and what it buys.
Shift the register for a landlord and an investor while keeping the same mark, type and palette.
Verify what you exported by looking at it, correct it, and say which slides you could not see.

stages.name: S8 — The tent-card variable-data print run
stages.goal: Turn the printer's flat PDF of last year's tent card into a working personalised template and produce a press-ready run for the new unit — one card per dish that actually has a photograph, plus proofs the client can sign off on screen.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Five decisions. (1) There is no native file, only a flat printed PDF, so the template must be reverse-engineered before anything can be personalised — and what the conversion actually yields in terms of separate text and picture frames is not knowable without inspecting it, so no field mapping can be promised in advance. (2) The stage-breaking one: the summary of the existing card's text is quietly incomplete — a run is dropped while its line break is kept, so the string still looks well-formed and every position after it is off by a constant. Validation passes, preparation reports success, and fields silently never print; only reconstructing the card's true text from the document itself, and independently confirming the placeholders landed before merging, catches it. (3) The run scope is a judgement call the agent must make and defend: four dishes have photographs, one of those is a low-resolution phone frame, and twelve dishes are on the menu. The agent decides how many cards ship, whether the phone frame can carry a card at print density given the photo area it chose, and says so. (4) The resolution requested at merge time is silently ignored, so a genuinely press-density file has to be produced by a different step than the obvious one. (5) The client's spreadsheet contains a prep-station column that is a kitchen routing field and does not belong on a customer-facing card; the price convention committed in S3 must be carried into the merge data or the printed cards contradict the poster on the same corner. Two constraints must be disclosed rather than solved: a template rebuilt from a flat PDF carries no bleed, and named press presets are unavailable.
subtasks: Turn the printer's PDF into a working layout document and inspect what it actually contains before promising any field mapping.
Establish the card's real existing text from the document itself and build the template on that, then confirm independently that every field you intended is genuinely there before you merge anything.

Prepare the merge data yourself from the client's spreadsheet: the dishes that ship, prices in the same format the rest of the kit uses, the customer-facing lines only, and each dish's own photograph bound to its own row.
Decide how many cards the run contains given the photography that exists and the resolution it has, and state the reason in the handover.
Produce the press file as one document, one dish per page, in menu order.
Produce screen proofs at print resolution for sign-off.
Confirm that each card carries its own dish and that the food reads cleanly on the card ground.
Tell the client and her printer exactly what the file is and is not, in terms the printer can act on.

stages.name: S9 — Handover: delivery, consistency sweep, launch pack, honest limits
stages.goal: Actually put the kit in the client's hands as one coherent, editable, shareable package she can launch from, with the reasoning written down, the campaign planned, the gaps named and the boundaries stated.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: [GRADER-ONLY] Three decisions. (1) Delivery: everything authored lives in the agent's own storage until it is deliberately shared with edit rights and collected into one place — the client's explicit ask ('so my son can open them and change a price') is unmet by producing the files, and an agent that stops at production has delivered nothing she can use. (2) Honesty: several things the brief implicitly assumes are not available on this route — pulling a flat file out of the editable documents, animating the social set, bleed on the reprinted card, a named press preset, and visually confirming every page of a multi-page document. The professional move is to name each one, say what she gets instead, and say what the printer or media owner must do. (3) Commercial judgement: she named $6,000 and a hard date and asked what to cut. Phasing the kit, telling her which dishes still need shooting and how to shoot them so they match, and writing the captions and the posting order are the difference between artwork and a launch — and none of it is design work. She also lived through four versions of one mark, so the consistency sweep across eleven artifacts is the deliverable she will actually check.
subtasks: Collect every deliverable into one named place and share each editable document with the client with edit rights, so she and her son can genuinely open and change them; hand over the source files too.
Sweep every artifact for one mark, one type system, one palette, one price format and one set of trading details, and fix any drift.
Write the direction rationale in the client's terms: her prices, her lunch hour, how far away the decision is made, who is reading and how fast.
Write the photographic parameter log, per frame, with the reason each frame needed different numbers.
Write a shot list for the dishes that still have no photograph — what to shoot, from where, in what light, at what distance — so the next batch matches the ones you graded.
Write the launch pack: caption copy in the languages you decided on, and a posting order across the weeks to opening and the first week trading, mapped to the pieces you built.
Write the phasing plan against her budget and her date: what ships for opening, what waits, what the next money should buy, and anything on her list you think is not worth doing at her size.

Write the limits note: what is editable and where, what she cannot get out of these files on this route and what she gets instead, what her printer must be told about the tent cards, and anything you could not visually confirm.
Index the element library so her son can find the right version of the mark for a given surface.
stages.feeds_into: Final delivery.

options_required: Three places where the client has explicitly asked to be shown alternatives and told which one you would pick, plus two scoping calls she has asked you to make and defend. (1) ART DIRECTION — three complete directions, one per slide of the direction board, each differing in photographic intent, palette logic and typographic voice, and each shown on a small full composition of the actual corner-window poster so she is choosing on the thing she would walk past. Commit to one and argue it against her prices, her thirty-five-minute lunch hour, how far away the decision gets made and what is on the same avenue — and say what the other two would have been right for. Three colour swaps of one layout is not three directions. (2) THE MARK — two candidate recoveries of the logo from the two files she sent, placed side by side on a dark ground, with a statement of which one you are shipping and what specifically fails in the other. Both must be real attempts, not a straw man. (3) POSTER LAYOUT — two A3 layouts that genuinely differ in how they make the price read before the name at distance; select one and state what the rejected one did worse against that test. (4) LANGUAGE — a per-surface rule for which language leads, which is secondary and where only one fits, with the alternative you rejected named and the reason given in terms of who is reading each surface. (5) RUN SCOPE — how many tent cards the run contains given the photography that exists, stated with the reason, and what the client should do about the rest. In all five, argue in her terms — price, distance, speed of decision, who is reading — not in design vocabulary.
element_reuse: [GRADER-ONLY] The engagement is built so recovery happens once and reuse happens across eleven artifacts, and so that every authored document is structurally dependent on at least two elements only the imaging chain can produce. THE MARK is recovered exactly once from whichever of the two logo-bearing files actually supports it, cleaned once (opaque plate removed, scaling box injected, counters opened), and split into exactly two shipping states by editing fill values on the cleaned vector so the geometry is identical in both. It is then placed in both outdoor pieces, the menu board, both window/door graphics, all three social canvases, all four paid units, the promo tile, every deck slide as a corner lockup, and the printed tent cards. Recovered badly, it is badly recovered in twelve places, and the client's stated pain becomes the failure mode. THE DISH ELEMENTS are prepared once from the corrected masters and reused across the three listing images, the promo tile, the paid square and — bound per row — the printed cards, so a separation that left a filled interior or a plate edge ships to press. THE TEXTURE PANEL is produced once at the largest size needed and reduced per surface, then reused as the ground field on the poster, the vertical story canvas and the deck cover; it is what makes those three read as one system, and it is a second connector-only dependency the grader can bind. THE TYPE EMBED is built once covering every face the whole kit uses, and every artifact writes its type from that one set of family references. THE CORRECTED MASTERS are the only photography in the engagement — every crop in every format descends from them, so the S1 grade decision is present in every visual deliverable. THE PRICE CONVENTION committed in S3 propagates into both outdoor pieces, the menu board, the social set, the paid units, the promo tile and the merge data for the printed cards. THE TRADING FACTS (address and cross-street, opening date, hours, phone, listing handle) propagate into every surface that carries them, and their inconsistency is the failure that actually costs the client customers.
failure_gates: [GRADER-ONLY] GRADING THE FOOD FOR THE WRONG PRICE BAND. The reflexive 'restaurant photography' move is a low-key, desaturated, closed-shadow, moody grade. At $12.50 a plate for a shift worker deciding on the sidewalk in five seconds, that is the wrong business's grade — it makes a generous plate look small and expensive. The correct read of the supplied price band and demographic is bright, open-shadowed and appetite-forward. Get it wrong and every photographic surface in the kit is visibly for a restaurant that does not exist.

[GRADER-ONLY] APPLYING ONE SET OF CORRECTIONS TO FOUR DIFFERENTLY-LIT FRAMES. Two frames were shot under warm interior lamps in the evening, one by a window at midday, one on a phone under mixed fluorescent. Identical parameters across them, or an independent automatic pass on each, leaves plates that visibly come from different restaurants — the exact complaint the client already made. It breaks most visibly in the deck and in the three-image listing set, where the frames sit side by side.

[GRADER-ONLY] MISSING THAT ONE FRAME IS A LOW-RESOLUTION PHONE CAPTURE WITH NO REFERENCE CARD. It cannot carry a print hero or a full-bleed card at print density without enlargement, and it has to be matched by eye with no anchor. An agent that treats all four frames as interchangeable either ships an enlarged mush to press or silently mismatches one dish.

[GRADER-ONLY] TRIAGING THE TWO LOGO-BEARING FILES WRONG. They are the same kind of file, neutrally named, and the small flat export is the one that looks easiest. It carries a baked-in shadow and resampling artifacts and cannot go to awning scale. The photographed one will not yield a mark by the route that works on a flat export; asking for the logo as an object returns the surface it sits on, and knocking the background off a ring-shaped mark returns a solid shape with the negative space filled. Every wrong route reports success and the failure is invisible until the mark is placed on a dark ground at size.

[GRADER-ONLY] SHIPPING THE TRACED MARK WITHOUT CLEANING IT. It arrives with an opaque full-canvas plate behind it and no intrinsic scaling box, and nothing warns about either. Placed as-is the mark sits in a visible rectangle on every dark ground in the kit and refuses to scale — the two things the client asked for by name.

[GRADER-ONLY] PRODUCING THE REVERSED MARK BY ADJUSTING A RASTER RATHER THAN BY EDITING THE VECTOR'S FILLS. Hue adjustment holds only at moderate adjacent-hue moves and cannot reach a clean knockout; taking that route also breaks the one-mark requirement, because the placed artwork is then a picture in some places and vector in others.

[GRADER-ONLY] REFERENCING THE PHOTOGRAPHY BY ADDRESS INSTEAD OF EMBEDDING IT. The layout route accepts an image reference, exports successfully, reports success and renders an empty box — including addresses on the platform's own hosts. Applied across the poster, the shelter face, the social set, the promo tile and the deck, this produces a complete, well-structured, entirely foodless launch kit for a restaurant whose whole pitch is the food.

[GRADER-ONLY] EMBEDDING THE HERO AT ITS PLACED SIZE. Text and vector stay resolution-independent but an embedded photograph is fixed at its placed pixel box, so a hero embedded at its layout size is soft at A3 and unusable at shelter scale. The correct move is to embed at a multiple of the placed box and disclose the effective resolution; the naive one looks correct on screen and is discovered at the printer.

[GRADER-ONLY] TAKING THE READY-MADE TEMPLATE ROUTE. It is the obvious shortcut for 'a poster and some social posts', and on this route a template cannot accept the client's own photography at all. Taking it means delivering a launch kit built on generic stock food to a client whose entire differentiator is that the plate in the picture is the plate you get.

[GRADER-ONLY] DECLARING CANVAS SIZES GLOBALLY INSTEAD OF PER-PIECE. Forcing one canvas across a multi-piece document collapses the three-format social set and the four paid units into repeats of one size. The client asked for a square, a vertical and a wide one and gets three squares.

[GRADER-ONLY] BUILDING ON EFFECTS THAT DO NOT SURVIVE. A glowing sign treatment, a soft-focus background, layered drop shadows, a repeating tiled background fill, or outlined display type are all natural reaches here. They are silently discarded on import — outlined type with a transparent fill disappears entirely, taking the headline with it, and a tiled background fill imports as an empty box. The export still succeeds.

[GRADER-ONLY] GUESSING NUMERIC TYPE WEIGHTS, OR BUILDING THE EMBED FROM UNLAUNDERED NAMES. Style names and weight numbers do not correspond consistently across families, so the reflexive regular weight can ship a Light body face on a poster whose only job is legibility at distance. And the brand sheet names a face that does not exist in the library; one unlaundered name in a single embed request fails the whole embed and discards every valid face with it.

[GRADER-ONLY] PUTTING TEXT, A LOGO OR A PRICE ON THE DELIVERY-LISTING IMAGES. The client quoted the platform's rule. Tiles built with branding get bounced or down-ranked and the opening-week listing goes live with a placeholder. The correct answer carries recognition on ground, colour and the cut of the food alone, and moves the price to the promo tile where it is permitted.

[GRADER-ONLY] DELIVERING THE LISTING IMAGES AS EDITABLE DOCUMENTS. The channel takes uploadable files; the layout route produces none. The imaging route does. An agent that authors them as layouts has produced something the client cannot upload.

[GRADER-ONLY] TRUSTING THE REPORTED TEXT WHEN REBUILDING THE TENT-CARD TEMPLATE. The summary of the existing card's text quietly omits a run while keeping its line break, so the string looks well-formed and every position after it is off by a constant. Validation passes, preparation reports success, and fields never appear in the printed run — discoverable only by opening the finished cards, after they have gone to the printer.
[GRADER-ONLY] PRODUCING THE PRESS FILE BY THE OBVIOUS ROUTE. The resolution requested at merge time is silently ignored, yielding a screen-resolution file that looks correct and prints soft.

[GRADER-ONLY] PRINTING THE KITCHEN ROUTING FIELD. The prep station is in the client's spreadsheet because her son typed the whole sheet. It is not customer-facing and no restaurant prints it on a table tent. An agent that merges every available column ships it.

[GRADER-ONLY] ACCEPTING A FREE ENLARGEMENT, OR CUTTING BEFORE REDUCING. A crop that overshoots the source quietly interpolates up to a limit and reports success, with the only signal buried in a returned note; and separating a camera-scale frame before reducing it can force exactly that at delivery size, because the separation step silently reduces oversized input and never restores it.

[GRADER-ONLY] LETTING THE PRICE FORMAT OR THE TRADING FACTS DRIFT. The poster, the board, the tiles, the ad units and the printed cards are all seen from the same sidewalk. Three renderings of $12.50, two versions of the opening date or a wrong cross-street is the same failure the client already suffered with four versions of the mark — and the trading facts are the ones that actually cost her customers.

[GRADER-ONLY] SCALING THE A3 UP FOR THE SHELTER. Different aspect, different viewing distance, different trim, supplied at a marked scale. A rescaled A3 is rejected by the media owner and looks wrong in the frame.

[GRADER-ONLY] DELIVERING A DECK WITHOUT ARITHMETIC. Rendering the supplied covers and rent without computing break-even and without a number on the ask produces a brand deck with a chart in it. The landlord does not care about the offer and the investor cannot act on an ask with no figure.

[GRADER-ONLY] STOPPING AT PRODUCTION. Everything authored sits in the agent's own storage until it is deliberately shared with edit rights and collected in one place. An agent that never shares has not delivered the one thing the client asked for by name.

[GRADER-ONLY] PROMISING WHAT THE ROUTE CANNOT DO, OR SILENTLY OMITTING IT. No flat file comes out of the editable documents, the reprinted card carries no bleed and no named press preset, no animated piece exists, and only the first page of a multi-page document can be visually confirmed. Naming these in the client's terms is the deliverable; quietly dropping them is the failure.

hardness_rationale: [GRADER-ONLY] The engagement is hard for a skilled human freelancer and hard for the agent, for different reasons that compound, and the breadth is load-bearing rather than decorative: this is what a real corner-restaurant launch actually ships, and the client's own stated pain — four versions of one mark — is a consistency failure that only exists across many surfaces. Depth is protected by two rules. First, every authored document carries a failure mode the others do not: the direction board must differ measurably across three roots and is the first place the multi-root visual-verification limit bites; the outdoor document is the only one at true physical trim, with the widest scale ratio, the heaviest embedded payload and a print-density decision made invisibly at embed time; the in-store document is the only one that must resolve a whole twelve-row price architecture as a structured table at queue distance under a bilingual rule; the social and paid documents carry the aspect extremes where a global canvas declaration collapses the set and where 320×50 forces a real sacrifice; the listing images are produced by an entirely different route with no type allowed, so recognition is carried by ground and cut alone; the deck must do arithmetic; and the tent-card run is a reverse-engineering job with a silent data defect in the middle. Second, nearly every stage's output is the next stage's input, so a wrong decision early is visible late and nowhere in between. The five sharpest gates are (a) the price band determining the photographic grade — the reflexive moody restaurant look is wrong here and wrong in every downstream piece; (b) the logo triage, where two same-kind, neutrally-named files need opposite treatments, the easier-looking one is the wrong source, and every wrong route reports success while producing a substrate blob, a solid disc, or a mushy shadow-contaminated trace; (c) the image-embedding decision, where referencing photography by address exports a complete, successful, foodless kit and embedding at placed size exports a poster that prints soft; (d) the merge-template reconstruction, where the reported existing text quietly omits a run, validation passes, preparation reports success, and fields silently never print; and (e) the resolution and scope triage on the phone frame, which the agent must discover by looking, since nothing names it. None of these can be caught without the agent inspecting its own rendered output, which it can do headlessly for the first piece of any document and structurally thereafter — and the honest handling of that split is itself scored, because crediting a visual loop the agent cannot run would be a false gate. Measurability is grader-side throughout: canvas geometry and root counts read from the export returns, reference-card channel spread measured on the retained card-bearing masters (with card exclusion checked separately on the deliverables, and the uncarded frame checked by patch agreement), resolved faces and numeric weights read from the exported structure, mark path sets compared after normalising for scale and translation, embedded-image intrinsic dimensions read out of the documents, page count equal to the agent's own row count, print density on the proofs, break-even arithmetic recomputed from the supplied workbook, and a scan for any enlargement note. The agent is never asked to read a pixel or a hex; it works by eye and reports the parameters it applied. why_not_a_vlm_one_shot: [GRADER-ONLY] A general vision-language model can produce a picture of a taqueria poster. It cannot produce this. Ask it for the kit and you get flat images: no editable document shared to the client with edit rights that her son can open and change a price in, no live text in a licensed typeface at a verifiably correct numeric weight, no vector mark with open counters that scales to an awning and reverses on a dark ground, no press-ready multi-page file whose page count equals the run the agent scoped with a different photograph bound to each page, no genuine structured table of twelve dishes a non-designer can edit, no editable chart, and no way to keep one recovered mark geometrically identical across twelve artifacts. It cannot do the recovery at all — pulling a stroke-accurate, counter-open, scalable mark out of a phone photograph of hand-painted door glass is an isolation-and-trace pipeline with a polarity decision in the middle and two silent defects to clean afterwards, not a description task; asked to 'redraw the logo' it invents a new one, which is exactly the failure the client already lived through. It cannot converge four differently-lit client photographs onto one white point against the reference material in three of them and report the settings it dialled per frame, because it has no editing surface and nothing to dial. It cannot notice that one frame is 1600px and therefore cannot carry a press card, because it does not have to respect a reduction-only chain. And critically, the difficulty here lives in failure modes that only exist once the artifacts are real: a photograph referenced by address that exports as an empty box, a hero embedded at its placed size that prints soft, a traced mark carrying an invisible opaque plate that only shows on a dark ground, a multi-format set collapsing to one canvas size, a template whose reported text is quietly short by one run so fields never print, listing images bounced by a channel rule about text. A one-shot generation has none of those failure modes because it never builds anything that could fail — which is another way of saying it never builds anything the client can launch with. The chained, dependent, self-inspecting, actually-delivered nature of the work is the task; a single generated image is the thing the client already has too many of.
