S1: image_auto_straighten for the tilt, image_apply_adjustments for per-frame exposure/temperature/tint/contrast/shadows, image_crop_to_bounds and image_crop_and_resize for delivery crops — reduction only, with metadata.tradeoffs the sole signal of both the silent 2× enlargement cap and the silent reduction on oversized input. S2: image_select_by_prompt at ink level (verified stroke-accurate on a printed mark with counters excluded), image_invert_selection for polarity, image_crop_to_bounds driven by returnBbox, image_vectorize, then local viewBox injection and removal of the full-canvas path 0. The two shipping mark states are produced by editing the cleaned SVG's literal fill hex — NOT by masked HSL, which is verified to hold only at moderate adjacent-hue moves and cannot reach a knockout; this also keeps the placed artwork vector everywhere, which is what V-A04 checks. Dish elements via image_remove_background (transparent, and with backgroundColor for flat-ground plates; alpha verified surviving both crop tools at png), with the reduction ordered BEFORE separation so the silent downscale cannot force a later enlargement. Texture panel via material-surface selection plus image_apply_monochromatic_tint / image_add_grain, delivered as a full-bleed placed panel, never a CSS repeating fill (verified: a background-image with an embedded source is dropped entirely). Reading the recovered ochre needs no eyedropper — image_vectorize emits literal fill hex in the SVG markup. S3: font_recommend once per role, font_styles for the true numeric weights, find_fonts to launder every name (including the fabricated one) into canonical form, get_fontkit_embed_url for ONE kit covering the whole engagement (25 families verified in one call), css_stack used verbatim. Note the connector's own documented substitution fallback (selected_font similarity) is verified broken and must not be relied on. AUTHORING (S3–S7): create_visual_design_express_skill → self-contained HTML → html_export_readiness_skill (mandatory before every export and every retry) → export_html_to_express, fully headless and synchronous. Relies on verified capabilities: multi-root documents in one call; mixed canvas sizes in one document (verified 1920×1080 and 1080×1080 side by side), which is what makes the social set, the paid set, the outdoor pair and the in-store set single documents; true physical canvases (297×420mm resolves to exactly 1123×1587px at 96dpi, pt sizes pass through) with the large-format pieces supplied at a declared reduction because that is how OOH and wall artwork actually ship; free-form absolute coordinate layout; inline SVG becoming native editable Express paths, which is how the daypart chart stays editable; real tables with per-cell backgrounds, strokes and text, which is how the twelve-row menu board and the deck's numbers stay editable; and photography embedded as data URIs — the ONLY form that renders, since every external address including the platform's own hosts becomes a blank placeholder. PAYLOAD: heroes are embedded at 2.5–3× their placed CSS box for print density (a ~3300px hero inside a 1123px box is ~290 effective dpi), which pushes past the 70KB inline advisory immediately; the verified escape is to upload the authored HTML itself via asset_initialize/finalize with media_type text/html and pass the returned *.adobe.com presignedAssetUrl as export_html_to_express's `url` (only *.adobe.com and *.claudeusercontent.com are accepted). Inline <svg> markup is preferred over a base64 data URI for the mark — verified ~25% smaller and the form the readiness skill wants. VERIFICATION: asset_search → asset_get_presigned_urls → asset_inline_preview returns the rendered FIRST root only, so the loop is genuinely visual for root 1 and structural (parsing slides[].html for placeholder sources, per-root canvas dimensions, resolved PostScript faces, present hz-text) for roots 2..N — the spec requires the agent to say so rather than claiming a loop it cannot run, and V-A22 checks the disclosure. LISTING IMAGES: produced entirely on the imaging route as flat 1200×1200 rasters (remove_background transparent or with backgroundColor onto the committed ground, then crop_and_resize down) because the channel takes uploadable files and this route has no flat export; the no-type rule makes that a feature, not a workaround. S8 PRINT: convert_pdf_to_indd on the printer's PDF, export_idml to inspect the true frame inventory and reconstruct the story text, generate_indd_mapping_prompt used for its frame inventory and as a validator but never trusted for its lossy textContent, prepare_indd_merge_template with the mapping passed as a JSON string, export_idml again to confirm placeholders actually landed, document_merge_data_layout to application/pdf for one press file with one record per page in row order (PDF order is verified correct; multi-record raster order is verified REVERSED and must not be used), with additionalImageFiles binding the S2 elements through an @-prefixed CSV column whose cells hold bare filenames, and document_render_layout for the 300-density proofs because outputSpecs.resolution is silently ignored at merge time. S9 DELIVERY: asset_create_folders + asset_copy_assets to collect, asset_share_link and asset_invite_collaborators to actually put the editable documents in the client's hands with edit rights — without which nothing has been delivered. NOTHING BANNED IS USED: no text-to-image, generative fill, AI object removal, background replacement by prompt, compositing, cartoonize, upscaling, OCR, watermark removal, video, audio, per-artboard named export, responsive layout, image replacement inside a template, or batch over ~20 files. image_generative_expand is explicitly EXCLUDED from every stage and named in V-A20: the project's own ground-truth doc bans it, and outpainting a client's food photograph fabricates food on a brand whose pitch is that the plate in the picture is the plate you get — the camera-scale declarations make every required crop reachable by reduction so it is never needed. NOT DESIGNED AGAINST: fill_text (non-deterministic, truncates, leaks label prefixes), animate_design (prose only, no artifact), create_firefly_board (a URL builder that persists nothing), variable QR fields (documented, validated, inert), download_design / suggest_type_palettes / get_type_palette / replace_image (absent from this host), the async video and vector families (their poll tools do not exist here), StockAsset orientation filters (always zero hits), and PDF presets and bleed on a PDF-derived template (rejected and unavailable — every print gate is stated as trim dimensions and effective resolution, and both limitations are disclosure requirements in V-A22). NO HUMAN WIDGET IS ON ANY CRITICAL PATH: search_design is not used at all, uploads go through the headless init/PUT/finalize path rather than the file picker, and the authoring skill's two AskUserQuestion branches (delivery destination; start from a stock template) are both answered explicitly and in character in the client brief's final paragraph, so a compliant agent has nothing to stop and ask.

engagement_title: Season 26 Kit Programme — archive recovery through committee-ready launch collateral
one_line_ask: Recover Ironside's house lettering and numerals from what survived the flood, build the Season 26 campaign identity on them, put three directions up and take one forward, then deliver the launch set: an A3 noticeboard poster with a real press file, a mixed-format social set, an online-store pair, a five-slide committee deck, and a personalised quote sheet for each of the six clubs currently in conversation.

brand_identity_additions.price_range: AGENT-FACING. Ex-VAT, as quoted on the phone. Route 1 — name and number heat-pressed onto shirts the club already owns: £9 per shirt, minimum order 6. Route 2 — full customisation of a club's own blank jerseys (house twill lettering and numbers, cut and stitched): from £34 per shirt. Route 3 — full custom Ironside kit, shirt + shorts + socks: £68–£92 per player for senior sizes depending on fabric weight and whether sleeve sponsors are printed; junior sizes £62–£82. A 16-player senior outfield pack (per-player kit plus one spare set) lands £1,150–£1,480. A 24-player junior academy pack lands £1,590–£2,050. Goalkeeper set £110. Training-bib set of 12 £96. Rush service — five working days instead of fifteen — adds 18%. Standard turnaround is 15 working days from artwork sign-off. No setup fee on repeat orders; the club's artwork stays on file. All figures exclude VAT at 20%, and clubs cannot reclaim it.
brand_identity_additions.positioning: AGENT-FACING. The workwear end of team kit, not the fashion end and not the bargain end. Ironside sells durability and a house lettering system nobody else in its bracket has: proprietary twill letterforms and numerals cut and stitched in-house, guaranteed legible for three seasons of machine washing or recut free. The pitch is 'this will still be readable in year three', against both cheap heat-transfer shops whose vinyl peels by Christmas and boutique kit labels charging triple on the strength of a photo shoot.
brand_identity_additions.demographics: AGENT-FACING. The buyer is almost never the player. It is a volunteer club kit secretary or a parent-committee treasurer, roughly 30–55, mid household income, doing this on a Tuesday evening after work. They are spending other people's money — subs, a raffle, a small local sponsor — and they will have to stand up in a clubhouse and justify the figure to eight other volunteers who all reckon they could have got it cheaper. They collect two or three competing quotes and compare them side by side on a table. They cannot reclaim VAT and they are the person who gets blamed if the invoice is bigger than the number the committee approved. Buying occasion is once a season, concentrated June to August, in a single committee-approved order of 16–24 units. Secondary buyer: junior academy coordinators ordering for age-group squads — same profile, more price-sensitive, more likely to reorder mid-season for new joiners. Ironside has about a ten-week window of visibility; after August nobody thinks about kit until the following May.
brand_identity_additions.competitive_set: AGENT-FACING. Local heat-transfer print shops undercutting on unit price with vinyl that cracks; national teamwear catalogues selling a stock template with a club badge dropped on it; and a small number of boutique bespoke-kit labels charging £180+ per shirt on art direction alone. Ironside sits deliberately between the first two and the third.
brand_identity_additions.design_implication: GRADER-ONLY — REFERENCE REGISTER ANALYSIS. NOT SHOWN TO THE AGENT. This paragraph is the answer key for the price-band gate; the agent receives price_range, positioning, demographics and competitive_set and must derive all of it. Correct register: prices present and specific, with a per-unit figure always shown alongside the whole-pack total, because the buyer's real problem is arguing a four-figure number to a room; the VAT position stated plainly, because the gap between an approved £1,150 and an invoiced £1,380 is how this brand loses a club and its league; evidence of durability (the stitch, the twill edge, the three-season guarantee) outranking aspiration; a limited flat ink budget of two or three spot colours with no gradients or metallics, which at this band signals 'we spend on the garment, not the brochure'; heavy, industrial, squarely-set type with the proprietary numerals as hero, because they are literally what the money buys. Correct handling of urgency: production lead time is honest and on-brand at this band ('order by [date] and it is on backs for the first fixture', derived from the stated 15-working-day turnaround) and is REQUIRED on the poster, at least one social unit and every quote sheet; discount urgency is not — percentage-off starbursts, strike-through pricing, SALE banners and countdown ribbons place Ironside with the vinyl shops and destroy the three-season claim. A correct answer distinguishes the two rather than avoiding dates altogether. Equally wrong at this band is the boutique treatment — vast white space, a small mark, a moody hero photograph, no price anywhere — which reads as unaffordable to a treasurer and gets the quote binned unread. Counterfactuals the grader uses to test whether the band is load-bearing: at £15-a-shirt fast turnaround the set would go price-led and loud with the number as the headline; at £300 bespoke the price would disappear and the set would become photography-led and spare. At £68–£92 with a four-figure pack total sold to a volunteer committee, the register is honest, dense, specific, and legible from four metres on a damp clubhouse noticeboard.

client_brief:
Marnie Oduya — Ironside Kit Works
Season 26 programme launch. Issued 4 May 2026.

Right, this is the big one for us, so I'll try to give you everything at once rather than drip-feeding it.

Ironside is six of us in a converted joinery unit. We customise team kit for amateur and junior clubs — mostly football, some rugby and netball. The thing that makes us different from the print shop two towns over is that we cut and stitch our own lettering and numbers in twill, in a house alphabet my dad drew when he set the place up in the nineties. Every other shop in our bracket buys in the same three sans-serif number sets from a catalogue. Ours are ours. They're squarer, they've got a proper flat-cut counter, and they survive three seasons of a washing machine, which is the entire reason clubs come back to us.

Here is the problem. That alphabet has never existed as artwork we can actually use. It lives as steel cutting dies on the bench and as printed reference sheets. When we've needed it for anything — a banner, an order form, the website — we've photographed a sheet and used the photo, and it looks like what it is. I've had three separate people tell me our own marketing makes our lettering look worse than it is, which is a hell of a thing to hear about the one thing we're actually good at.

So: first job is to get that alphabet back as proper reusable artwork, once, properly, so we never have to do this again. I've dug through the archive and what survived the flood in the old unit and the laptop that died is in the folder — they're all ours, they came off different equipment at different times over about a decade, and I couldn't tell you what's in any of them because nobody ever labelled anything. Open them and work out what you've actually got. Tell me, in writing, what each one is and what you did with it and why. If you end up telling me one of them is no use to us, fine, but I want the reason, and I want to know what you did instead — I care about the result, but I also have to be able to explain to my brother why we paid for something that isn't in the final work.

What I need out of the alphabet at the end is not a picture of an alphabet. Our sign-maker needs to be able to set a club's name from it — WEXBRIDGE ATHLETIC, six-inch letters, cut in vinyl for a clubhouse board — without redrawing anything or opening a drawing program to chop a sheet into pieces. And I want to be able to set a squad number in it on an order form. So hand it over in whatever form makes that actually possible, and tell him how to space it.

Second job is that we're launching the Season 26 programme. Clubs order in June, July and August and then they don't think about us again until the following May, so we get about ten weeks and we have to be visible everywhere at once. Season kicks off the weekend of 15 August. I want to start posting the first week of June. I need the three directions from you by 15 May and the full set by 5 June. Budget for the package is £6,800, half on the directions, half on delivery.

What I need, and everything here has to be obviously the same thing:

A poster for clubhouse noticeboards. A3. It has to work pinned behind glass with three other notices around it and be readable from across a room by someone walking past. This is the piece that has to carry the lettering. I'll also blow one up for our own shop window, so make sure it still holds together bigger and don't hang it on anything that only works when you're standing right in front of it. And I need a file our print shop will actually take — not a screen file, a proper print one.

A social set. One square feed post, one vertical story, and one wide unit for a paid placement — the agency told me 1200 by 628 for that one, they were specific. Same campaign, three shapes, and I don't want three unrelated designs — I want someone scrolling to recognise the second one from having seen the first.

Something for the online store. Two things really: a wide banner across the top of the shop page, and a square that explains what customisation actually means, because half our enquiries are people who don't know the difference between what we do and what a vinyl transfer shop does. That square has to still make sense shrunk down to about 200 pixels in a listing grid, because that's how people see it.

A short deck for Dev, who does our club visits. Five slides, shown off a laptop on a clubhouse table. He needs the pricing on there properly — all three ways of buying from us, with the actual figures, because kit secretaries always ask and he always ends up drawing it on a napkin and getting it wrong. Something visual that makes the durability argument would be good too, and it has to be readable across a table in about three seconds.

And a quote sheet. We've got six clubs mid-conversation right now and each needs their own, printed, A4. Last season we did them by hand in Word and they looked like a hostage note, and one of them went out with the wrong total on it. I've put last year's in the folder as a PDF because the original file is long gone. Everything a treasurer needs to argue it in a room has to be on there — I've listed what in the copy deck. And put the club's own name on it in our lettering. That's the whole pitch, sat on the table next to two quotes from shops who can't do it.

On direction: don't show me one idea. Show me a few properly different ways this could go, tell me which one you'd back and why, and then build that one out. I'd rather argue with you about a choice than nod along to the only thing on the table. I'm away the fortnight after the directions land, so back your own pick and build it — but write me the case, and tell me what I'd have to say to change your mind.

I also need a line. Something Dev can say on a doorstep and I can put across the top of the poster, and captions we can actually post with, and a rough order for posting them across the ten weeks. I'm not going to write that myself and I'll only make it worse.

Two things I feel strongly about. First, the money has to be on the work. A kit secretary is spending the club's money and then has to defend the figure to a committee of people who all reckon they'd have found it cheaper. If our material is coy about price it gets thrown away; if it looks like a discount leaflet, we look like the shop whose numbers peel off by Christmas. We're neither. And be straight about VAT — clubs can't claim it back, and if a committee approves one number and the invoice is bigger, that's the last order we get from them. Second, what we sell is that it lasts. Whatever you make should feel like it came out of the same workshop as the product — solid, honest, not fussy, spending nothing on decoration it doesn't need. If it looks expensive to produce, a treasurer assumes they're paying for it.

Photography: we have nothing usable, so source it, and please make sure it's properly licensed because we did get a letter about that once. One thing though — our shirts are plain until we put the lettering on. Anything you use has to be a blank with nobody else's name, badge or sponsor block on it. I'm not putting another manufacturer's shirt on our own shop page, and I'm not having a league badge on there we've no right to.

Handover, and this matters as much as the work: we've got Adobe Express in-house. Hand it over as live Express files we can open and export ourselves, plus your source files, so I can change a date and a price next season without coming back to you. And write me the export settings for each piece — what size, what format, what the print shop needs — because I'll forget. I do not want any of this sitting on a stock template; every other shop's stuff looks like that and that's the whole problem I'm paying you to fix.

WHAT'S IN THE FOLDER

— The archive files: ref_01.png, ref_02.png, ref_03.png, ref_04.png. Same folder, no labels, no order.
— last_season_quote.pdf — last year's quote sheet, A4.
— clubs.csv — the six live conversations.
— copy_deck.txt — reproduced below so nothing gets lost.

COPY DECK (verbatim)

Three ways to buy:
1. NAME AND NUMBER ON YOUR OWN SHIRTS — £9 per shirt. Heat-pressed house lettering onto shirts you already have. Minimum order 6.
2. CUSTOMISATION OF YOUR CLUB'S BLANKS — from £34 per shirt. Your blank jerseys, our twill lettering and numbers, cut and stitched.
3. FULL CUSTOM IRONSIDE KIT — £68–£92 per player, senior. £62–£82 per player, junior. Shirt, shorts and socks. 16-player senior pack £1,150–£1,480. 24-player junior academy pack £1,590–£2,050.
Add-ons: goalkeeper set £110. Training bibs, set of 12, £96.

Terms line (must appear wherever prices appear): "All prices exclude VAT at 20%. Minimum order 6 shirts. Standard turnaround 15 working days from artwork sign-off; five working days available at +18%. No setup fee on repeat orders — your artwork stays on file with us."

Everything the quote sheet has to carry: club name, league, squad size, the pack we've quoted, the per-shirt figure, the pack subtotal, the VAT line, the total including VAT, lead time and the rush option, minimum order, the date we quoted, the date the quote runs out, and the rep's name with his direct number and email.

stages.name: Stage 0/1 — Session prerequisites, archive triage and mark recovery [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Establish the session (mandatory connector init, account type), then determine what each of the four unlabelled archive rasters actually is and recover Ironside's letter set and numeral set as clean two-colour vector artwork with open counters — composing the numeral set from more than one source where the primary source is damaged.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: Four files arrive under neutral names, all rasters, nothing in the brief or the spreadsheet indicating which is which. ref_01 is a flat scan of the numeral sheet, but ink bleed has closed the counters of two numerals. ref_02 is a photograph of the letter sheet on a workbench under warm uneven light, with a fold shadow crossing three glyphs. ref_03 is a close photograph of a finished jersey collar carrying a stitched trim device. ref_04 is a softer, lower-quality phone capture of the same numeral sheet — worse overall, but the two bled numerals are clean in it. The agent must decide: that ref_01 and ref_04 are the same artefact captured twice and must be COMBINED rather than one being chosen over the other; that ref_02 needs materially different exposure and contrast decisions from a flat scan, and that its fold-shadowed glyphs are a per-glyph judgement — salvage or rebuild — that must be made glyph by glyph and reported; and that ref_03 carries no traceable artwork and its device must be authored rather than salvaged, a call the client has NOT pre-authorised and which must be argued in the handover. It must further decide how to name the thing it is selecting: asking for the sheet, or the emblem on the sheet, pulls the selection to the substrate and yields a paper-shaped blob that still reports success; naming the ink's own colour, medium and form returns the strokes.
subtasks: Call adobe_mandatory_init before any Adobe tool, then get_account_type and confirm 'auth'.
Upload all four archive rasters headlessly (initialize / PUT / finalize) and preview every one before any operation. Write down what each is and what treatment it needs, with reasons.

Bring each recoverable sheet to a clean high-contrast state by eye — the workbench photograph needs different exposure, contrast and warmth decisions from the flat scan, and the low-quality phone capture different again. Report the parameters dialed on each.
Select the printed ink itself on each sheet, not the paper it sits on; confirm by looking at the returned mask that the counters came back excluded rather than filled; take the returned bbox.
Invert the mask before tracing so the trace yields a positive mark rather than a field with the glyphs knocked out of it.
Crop each mask to the artwork's own bounds using the returned geometry, not by eye.
Trace the prepared plates to vector.

Decide per damaged glyph — the two bled numerals, the three fold-shadowed letters — whether it is recoverable from the second capture, recoverable with local repair, or must be redrawn to match the house alphabet. Record every glyph rebuilt and why.
Record the decision on the collar photograph: what it is, why nothing in it can be traced, and what will be authored instead.
stages.feeds_into: Stage 2, and through it every one of the five authored surfaces and the six merged quote sheets. A substrate-shaped mask here puts a paper blob where the alphabet should be in five documents; a badly-judged glyph rebuild is visible on the poster and on the quote sheet of any club whose name contains it.

stages.name: Stage 2 — Vector hygiene, the glyph-level element kit, and the campaign ink plates [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Turn raw traces into a genuinely usable, glyph-addressable alphabet the client's sign-maker can set words from, plus the campaign ink plates and the authored collar trim device.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: Raw traced output is not placeable artwork and nothing in the toolchain says so: it carries no scaling information, its first path is an opaque full-canvas rectangle that will sit as a white or black box over any coloured ground, and its counters may survive as separate opaque fills rather than as holes — all three defects are invisible in the file and only appear when the mark is placed at a different size on a colour. Beyond fixing those, the agent must decide what 'reusable' actually means for this client: one SVG containing 26 letters is a picture of an alphabet and fails the stated job, so the kit has to be decomposed into individually addressable glyphs with a naming convention and enough metric information (cap height, numeral height, baseline, recommended letter gap) for someone to set a word without redrawing. It must also decide the campaign ink set — how many flat spot colours a shop that prints in flat spot colours should be spending, and which — and produce the numeral system in each, all derived from the one recovered mask.
subtasks: Retrieve the traced files locally and inspect their structure.
Inject scaling information; remove the full-canvas ground path; neutralise any residual opaque counter fills so the counters are genuinely open.
Decompose the traces into individually addressable glyphs on a stated naming convention, and repair or redraw the damaged glyphs identified in Stage 1.
Write the metrics note: cap height, numeral height, baseline, recommended letter gap, and the ink hexes.
Choose the campaign ink set and produce the numeral system as flat plates in each ink, every plate filled through the single Stage-1 numeral mask.
Look at each plate and confirm it reads as the intended flat ink, and report the colour values used.
Author the collar trim device seen in the third archive file as vector, at the proportions the campaign needs.
connector_tools: Bash (local SVG inspection, hygiene, glyph decomposition, rasterisation)
stages.feeds_into: Stages 5, 6, 7 and 8. The same corrected mark is placed on the comps, the poster, all three social roots, both store roots and the deck; the glyph kit is what makes the per-club name plates in Stage 8 possible at all.

stages.name: Stage 3 — Type system for the campaign [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Choose, verify and license a working typographic system — a display voice and a text voice — that sits with the recovered proprietary lettering rather than competing with it, survives at four metres on a noticeboard and holds a dense price table at 9–11pt.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: The pairing is entirely the agent's: the recommendation surface returns candidates per role and explicitly refuses to pair, so which display face sits beside a squared industrial twill alphabet without fighting it or vanishing next to it, and which text face carries fifteen fields of quote data at small size, is judgement. The agent must also decide to establish the true numeric weight of every style per family rather than assuming the conventional value, and to launder every name into the exact form the embed requires before requesting it.
subtasks: Work the display role and the text role separately against the brief's register.
Shortlist at least two complete pairings and state what each would do to the brand at this price band.
Commit to one and say why the other was rejected; the rejected one must be a real contender.
Establish the true numeric weight of every style to be used, per family.
Validate every name, then build ONE licensed embed covering every face the whole campaign will use.
Write the type system down as roles — display, headline, subhead, body, price figure, caption, table cell — with family, numeric weight, size and tracking for each, crediting foundry and designer.
stages.feeds_into: Stages 5, 6 and 7 — one embed and one role table govern all five authored documents. A wrong weight or a name in the wrong form falls back silently and the whole set ships in the wrong voice.

stages.name: Stage 4 — Imagery: source, vet, license, prepare [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Assemble the campaign's photographic layer from properly licensed, brand-safe material and prepare each frame to one consistent look, including a clean product cutout and a durability close-up that carries the three-season claim.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: There is no client photography, so the agent decides what this brand's imagery is even for: at this band the evidence shot — stitch, twill edge, fabric weave — earns its place and the aspirational lifestyle shot does not. It must also act as an art buyer: teamwear stock routinely carries manufacturer marks, sponsor blocks and league badges, the client has explicitly ruled those out, and nothing in the connector can remove one — so frames must be inspected and rejected, and the rejections reported. It must bring frames shot under different lighting to one look with divergent per-frame corrections rather than one global move, reach each destination ratio without enlarging anything — which for at least one frame means extending the canvas rather than cropping into the subject — and prepare each image at the pixel size its placement actually occupies, because everything must be embedded and payload is finite.
subtasks: Search and license a small set covering a plain blank jersey suitable for a product treatment, a close detail carrying stitch and fabric texture, and a wider situational frame.
Inspect every candidate before licensing and reject any carrying a third-party mark, sponsor block or league badge; report what was rejected and why.
Confirm each licensed frame is genuine photography at camera scale and exclude anything flagged as AI-generated.
Bring the set to one look by eye with per-frame exposure, contrast, warmth and saturation decisions; report the parameters applied to each.
Produce the product cutout on a single flat studio ground.
Reframe each prepared image to the ratio its destination needs without enlarging it, extending canvas only where a straight crop would clip the subject.
Check every reframe for quiet interpolation and redo any that took it.
Downscale each finished image to the pixel width its placement box actually occupies at the target canvas's own scale, and prepare it in the form the layout stage can embed.
stages.feeds_into: Stages 5, 6 and 7. An image referenced rather than embedded arrives as an empty grey box in every layout and every export still returns success.

stages.name: Stage 5 — Campaign line, three directions, and a defended pick [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Write the campaign's verbal idea, then put three genuinely different ways of running Season 26 in front of the client as comparable comps that each survive a change of shape, and commit to one with an argument.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: There is no line in the copy deck and the client has explicitly asked for one — a campaign held together only by a colour and a typeface is not a campaign, and the social set's stated job (recognise the second from having seen the first) is carried by the line as much as by the mark. Then the three directions have to be three systems, not one layout in three colours: each must declare and demonstrate a different carrier — the recovered numerals, the durability evidence, or the price argument — differ in photographic weight, and differ in how they handle the money. Each must be shown on two canvases so that a direction has to survive reflow, which a recolour cannot fake. The pick must be defensible specifically at £68–£92 a shirt with a four-figure pack total sold to a volunteer treasurer who cannot reclaim VAT; a direction that would be right at a much lower or much higher band is a wrong answer here and the justification has to show the agent knows which is which.
subtasks: Write the campaign line and the guarantee line as they will actually be set, plus three social captions and a posting order across the ten-week window.
Develop three distinct campaign systems, each declaring its carrier element, its imagery weight and its treatment of pricing.
Author all three in one document, each as a 1080x1080 comp AND a reduced-scale A3 comp at 561x794, so the client sees each direction in two shapes side by side.
Render-check what actually landed and correct anything that differs from the intent before presenting.

Write the recommendation: which one, why, what it does for a kit secretary who has to defend the number, citing specific figures from the price list and specific buyer behaviour; what each rejected direction would have signalled at this band; and what the client would have to say to change the pick.
State what would change if the band were materially lower or higher.
stages.feeds_into: Stages 6, 7 and 8 — the chosen system's grid, palette, type roles, line and treatment of price govern everything remaining.

stages.name: Stage 6 — Rollout A: the A3 noticeboard poster, as an editable file AND a press file [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Build the campaign's most visible surface at true physical dimensions, deliver it as a live editable document the client can change next season, and produce an actual print-resolution file the client's print shop will take.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: The agent must decide the poster's read order for someone walking past at four metres behind glass with three other notices around it, and hold that read order when the same artwork is enlarged for a shop window — so nothing load-bearing can depend on being read close up. It must decide where the per-unit figure and the pack total sit given that the buyer's job is to defend a number, and whether and how to state an order-by date derived from the stated turnaround without tipping into discount urgency. It must also decide how to get a genuinely printable file out of a toolchain whose Express surface exports nothing: the same authored HTML has to be routed a second way to reach print resolution, which is a different production route from every other surface in the engagement.
subtasks: Author the A3 poster at true physical dimensions with the recovered lettering carrying the piece, the campaign line set, the price information placed where a defending buyer finds it, and an honest order-by date.
Embed every image; route the document by hosted URL rather than inline once it exceeds the inline threshold; never drop or shrink imagery to squeeze under it.
Export to a live Express document, render-check it, identify anything dropped or moved, fix and re-export.
Produce the press file from the same HTML by a print route rather than an Express export, at 300 dpi A3.
Confirm the type landed in the intended faces and weights rather than falling back.

stages.name: Stage 7 — Rollout B: social set, online-store pair, and the five-slide committee deck [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Roll the chosen system across the remaining screen surfaces without any of them becoming a redesign, and give the rep a deck that replaces his napkin.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: The agent must decide what is invariant across three social shapes and two store shapes — the mark, the ink set, the line, the price device, the type roles — and what is allowed to reflow, because the client's stated test is recognition, not variety. The store square and the store banner do different jobs: one has to teach a stranger the difference between stitched customisation and a vinyl transfer using the recovered system as its subject and still read at 200px in a listing grid; the other is a shop-page banner. For the deck, the agent must decide how to present three routes to buy that are not three tiers — one has no pack total at all — so a treasurer can compare them and quote one back, and must decide what durability evidence to visualise and in what form, readable across a table in about three seconds.
subtasks: Author the social set as one document with three roots at 1080x1080, 1080x1920 and 1200x628, each carrying its own canvas size, holding the campaign recognisable across all three.
Author the store document as two roots: a 1080x1080 customisation explainer built from the recovered letter and numeral system, and a 1600x600 shop-page banner carrying the product cutout.
Author the five-slide deck at 1920x1080 in one document with per-slide titles taken from the slides themselves.
Build the three ways to buy as a genuine table with the actual figures and the terms line, each route carrying a per-shirt figure and, where one exists, a pack total.
Build the durability argument as a native vector chart or diagram, sized to be read across a table.
Carry the type roles, ink set, line and mark across without redesigning them.
Render-check every page that carries a photograph, the recovered mark or the price device, and fix what dropped.
stages.feeds_into: Stage 8 — the deck's pricing content and the finished look set the content and register of the quote sheet.

stages.name: Stage 8 — Personalised per-club quote sheets from last season's flat artwork [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Turn the client's flat PDF of last season's quote sheet into a working personalised A4 layout and produce one print-resolution sheet per club, each carrying that club's full commercial detail and that club's own name set in the recovered alphabet.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: No native layout file survives, so the agent must reconstruct one and decide where each of fourteen fields belongs inside it — and the inventory it is handed of that reconstructed document is quietly incomplete, so any placement computed from what it is told rather than from the document's own contents will land some fields and silently drop others while every response reports success. The agent must decide to verify the reconstructed layout against itself before merging and again after. It must also decide how to make the per-club name plate: the name has to be composed from the glyph kit built in Stage 2, at consistent metrics, including glyphs that were damaged in the archive and repaired or redrawn — and bound per row into a graphic frame that exists in the converted document. Finally it must decide how these are delivered so a rep hands the right sheet to the right club, knowing that one of the available output routes returns its files in an order that does not match the rows.
subtasks: Reconstruct a working layout from the supplied flat quote-sheet artwork and confirm it exposes at least one usable graphic frame.
Establish what the reconstructed document actually contains — its true story text and its image frames — from the document itself, not from a summary of it.
Compose each club's name plate from the glyph kit, at the metrics stated in Stage 2, and rasterise it for binding.

Build the merge data: every field the copy deck lists, including the VAT line, the VAT-inclusive total, the quote date, the validity date, lead time and rush, minimum order, and the rep's direct contacts, plus the name-plate image column.
Map the fields, then confirm every placeholder is genuinely present before merging anything.
Merge the six clubs and render at print resolution.
Confirm one club per page in spreadsheet order with no missing fields and no mismatched name plate.
Deliver individually named single-club files by a route whose record identity is guaranteed.
connector_tools: Bash (unzip and read the exported IDML story text; compose and rasterise name plates)
stages.feeds_into: Handover — the last deliverable and the one most likely to ship silently broken, because every step of it reports success.

stages.name: Stage 9 — Handover: export instructions and the decisions log [GRADER-ONLY reference solution]
stages.goal: Make the package usable by the client after the freelancer is gone, and make every judgement in the engagement auditable.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: The client cannot export from a connector she does not have, and the Express surface produces no files — so the agent must decide to tell her, per piece, exactly what to export and at what settings, rather than quietly handing over documents and hoping. It must also decide how much of its own reasoning to expose: the archive verdicts, the glyphs it rebuilt, the frames it rejected on branding grounds, the parameters it dialed, and the direction it argued for.
subtasks: Write the export-and-handover sheet: per piece, the format, the size, the destination and what the print shop needs, plus the note that the Express layouts are live text and vector and export at any resolution.

Write the decisions log: what each archive file turned out to be and what was done with it; which glyphs were repaired and which redrawn, and why; which licensed frames were rejected and why; the per-frame image corrections and the ink values dialed; the type pairing decision and the rejected alternative; the direction pick, its justification and what would change it.
State plainly which deliverables are editable documents and which are finished files.

options_required: Two required option sets, at different altitudes, plus one running judgement that behaves like a third. (1) TYPOGRAPHY, Stage 3: the recommendation surface returns candidates per role and refuses to pair, so the agent must assemble at least two complete display-plus-text pairings, state what each would do to the brand at £68–£92 a shirt sold to a volunteer committee, commit to one, and say why the other was rejected. The rejected pairing must be a real contender, not a straw man; a grader who cannot imagine the rejected pairing shipping marks it as one. (2) CAMPAIGN DIRECTION, Stage 5: three genuinely different systems, each declaring its carrier element — the recovered numerals, the durability evidence, or the price argument — and each presented on TWO canvases in one document, a 1080x1080 and a reduced-scale A3, so a direction has to survive a change of shape. They must differ in photographic weight and in how they handle the money. The agent then picks one and defends it specifically against this band and this buyer, citing at least two exact figures from the price list and at least one stated buyer behaviour, saying what each rejected direction would have signalled — one of them should be recognisably right at a much lower band and one at a much higher one — and saying what the client would have to say to change the pick. Three recolours of one layout is a fail; three layouts that only exist as squares is a fail, because a square proves nothing about a system. The pick then binds: everything in Stages 6, 7 and 8 must be built in the chosen system. (3) The running judgement: every glyph the archive damaged is a small option set of its own — recover from the second capture, repair locally, or redraw to match the house alphabet — and the agent must choose per glyph and say which it chose. Some of those glyphs appear in club names on the printed quote sheets, so the choice is visible on a page handed across a table.
element_reuse: The alphabet is extracted once, corrected once, and decomposed once — and then everything else in the engagement is made of it. The corrected numerals are the hero of the A3 poster and its press file, the recognisable constant across all three social shapes, the entire subject of the customisation explainer, and the display voice on the deck's opening and closing slides. The same single numeral mask, never re-extracted, is filled through to produce every campaign ink plate. The glyph kit is what makes the per-club name plates possible at all: each club's name is composed letter by letter from those glyphs, at the metrics published in the same kit, and bound per row into the six printed quote sheets — which means a glyph the agent chose to redraw in Stage 2 is sitting on a page in front of a committee in Stage 8, and a glyph it chose to salvage badly is sitting there too. The collar trim device, authored once because nothing in the collar photograph can be traced, recurs as the campaign's rule or divider on every surface. One licensed type embed serves all five authored documents. One prepared photographic set serves the poster, the social set, the store banner and the deck. One campaign line appears unchanged on every visual piece. The consequence is that this engagement has a small number of places where something can go wrong and a large number of places where it becomes visible: an uncorrected trace puts an opaque rectangle over the design in five documents and six printed sheets, a substrate-shaped mask puts a paper blob where the alphabet should be everywhere at once, a wrong numeric weight ships the entire campaign a step too light, and an alphabet delivered as one flat sheet instead of addressable glyphs makes the per-club personalisation — the single most persuasive thing on the quote sheet — impossible to build.
failure_gates: [GRADER-ONLY] Treating the archive as a set of interchangeable files. Two captures are of the same numeral sheet and must be combined, because the primary capture has lost two glyphs to ink bleed and the secondary one — worse in every other respect — is the only clean source for them. Choosing one capture and discarding the other loses two numerals from the client's master artwork, and nothing in any tool response says so.

[GRADER-ONLY] Preparing a photographed sheet with the same exposure and contrast decisions used on a flat scan. The warm uneven gradient and the fold shadow drag paper tone and bench into the trace, and the hero of the poster becomes a rectangle with letters faintly inside it.

[GRADER-ONLY] Naming the substrate instead of the ink when isolating the artwork. Asking for the sheet, or the emblem on the sheet, returns a card-shaped mask; asking for the printed ink's own colour, medium and form returns the strokes. Both report success and both look plausible in the response.
[GRADER-ONLY] Skipping the polarity correction before tracing. The uncorrected trace yields a solid field with the glyphs knocked out of it — a black box delivered as the client's master artwork.

[GRADER-ONLY] Shipping the raw trace as the reusable element: no scaling information, an opaque full-canvas ground path as its first path, and counters that may survive as opaque fills rather than holes. None of the three is visible in the file; all three appear the moment the mark is placed at a different size on a colour.

[GRADER-ONLY] Delivering the alphabet as a picture of an alphabet. One SVG containing 26 letters satisfies every hygiene check and fails the client's stated primary requirement, and makes the per-club name plates in Stage 8 unbuildable.

[GRADER-ONLY] Trying to salvage the collar photograph as artwork. A photographed garment gives an opaque silhouette or a mesh of fabric-texture paths, and either one dropped into the collateral reads as mud. The client has NOT pre-authorised rebuilding it; deciding to author the device instead, and arguing it, is the agent's call.
[GRADER-ONLY] Referencing licensed photography by address rather than embedding it. Every image arrives as an empty grey box, every export returns success, nothing warns.

[GRADER-ONLY] Dropping or shrinking imagery to squeeze a document under the inline payload threshold instead of routing it as a hosted document. A silent quality failure that passes every structural check.

[GRADER-ONLY] Assuming conventional numeric weights instead of establishing them per family, or writing typeface names in the form they were returned rather than the form the embed requires. Either ships the whole campaign in the wrong voice with no error anywhere.

[GRADER-ONLY] Designing to the wrong price band. Percentage-off starbursts, strike-throughs or countdown devices place Ironside with the vinyl shops and destroy the durability claim; vast white space with a small mark, a moody hero and no price reads as unaffordable to a treasurer. Both are coherent, well-executed, wrong answers.

[GRADER-ONLY] Confusing production lead time with discount urgency. Omitting any order-by date fails the job — a June noticeboard poster for a business with a fifteen-working-day turnaround and a 15 August season start has no call to action without one. Putting a countdown ribbon on it fails differently.
[GRADER-ONLY] Presenting three variants rather than three directions, or presenting three directions only as squares so that nothing is proved about how any of them reflows.
[GRADER-ONLY] Letting the three social shapes become three designs. The client's stated test is that someone who saw the first recognises the second.

[GRADER-ONLY] Licensing a jersey that carries a manufacturer mark, sponsor block or league badge. The client ruled it out explicitly, nothing in the toolchain can remove it, and it is the exact thing she got a letter about.

[GRADER-ONLY] Building the quote-sheet field placements from the inventory the toolchain hands back rather than from the document's own contents. That inventory silently omits a run of text while keeping its line break, so every position after the omission is wrong by a fixed amount, validation passes clean, preparation reports success, and fields are simply absent from all six printed sheets.
[GRADER-ONLY] Requesting print resolution at the merge step, where it is silently ignored, instead of rendering the merged document as a separate step.

[GRADER-ONLY] Naming per-club output files by their position in the returned list for the raster route — the returned order does not match the row order, and the rep hands the wrong club its own quote.
[GRADER-ONLY] Letting a reframe quietly enlarge a licensed photograph. The interpolation is reported only as an aside and shows up as softness at A3.
[GRADER-ONLY] Stalling on the authoring skill's delivery question when the client has already answered it in the brief, or letting a layout drift responsive and arm the regeneration gate.
[GRADER-ONLY] Treating a successful export as fidelity, or treating the first-page render as coverage of a multi-page document.
traps: [GRADER-ONLY] The four archive files are ref_01.png, ref_02.png, ref_03.png, ref_04.png — same folder, same extension, neutral scheme, nothing in the brief or the spreadsheet indicating which is which. ref_01 is a flat scan of the numeral sheet with ink bleed that has closed the counters of two numerals. ref_02 is a photograph of the letter sheet on a workbench, warm uneven light, a fold shadow crossing three glyphs. ref_03 is a close photograph of a finished jersey collar. ref_04 is a soft phone capture of the SAME numeral sheet as ref_01 — worse overall, and the only clean source for the two bled numerals.

[GRADER-ONLY] No tilt is planted anywhere. The rectification tool's behaviour on a sheet of paper on a workbench is unverified on this host, so the differentiator between the scan and the photograph is the warm uneven gradient and the fold shadow, both of which the adjustment tool genuinely handles and both of which force divergent per-frame prep.

[GRADER-ONLY] Three of the six club names contain a glyph that falls under the fold shadow on ref_02, and one contains a numeral that is bled on ref_01. Whatever the agent decided about those glyphs in Stage 2 is printed on a page handed to a committee in Stage 8.

[GRADER-ONLY] Selection prompt wording is the entire gate on both sheets and the failure is silent: naming the substrate returns the paper, naming the ink's colour and medium returns the strokes, and both come back as a valid mask with a plausible pixel count.
[GRADER-ONLY] Mask polarity before tracing: one inversion is the difference between a positive mark and a field with the glyphs knocked out. Both trace successfully.

[GRADER-ONLY] Traced output always carries an opaque full-canvas rectangle as its first path and never carries scaling information; counters may additionally survive as separate opaque fills rather than as holes. None of it is mentioned anywhere and none of it is visible until the mark is placed on a coloured ground.

[GRADER-ONLY] No image can be placed into an authored layout by address — not even an address produced by the connector's own image tools. Everything must be embedded. The failure mode is an empty grey box and a completely successful export.

[GRADER-ONLY] Embedded photography pushes documents past the inline advisory threshold, so they must be routed as hosted documents rather than truncated; the naive escape is to shrink or drop the imagery, which passes every structural check.

[GRADER-ONLY] Typeface names are returned in one form and required in another, and the required form never appears in the returned name. One unvalidated name discards the entire embed request including the valid names.

[GRADER-ONLY] Numeric weights are not standard across families — the conventional regular value is the light cut in some families — so assuming rather than establishing ships the campaign a step too light with no warning.

[GRADER-ONLY] Anchoring an auto-sized element from the right or bottom edge, or wrapping a vector element in a container with no explicit dimensions, collapses it to zero width and throws its contents off the canvas. This is exactly a mark-plus-headline composition.

[GRADER-ONLY] Successful export is not fidelity: stroked and outlined type, blurs, blend modes, underlines, multi-column text and all but the first layer of a stacked shadow are dropped silently. A direction whose distinctiveness rests on any of those exports clean and arrives stripped.
[GRADER-ONLY] The rendered preview of a multi-page document shows page one only. Seventeen authored pages exist across five documents; two of them are page one.

[GRADER-ONLY] The authoring skill's own policy asks the user how to deliver the design and whether to start from a stock template. The client brief pre-answers both. An agent that asks anyway stalls a headless run on a question already answered.

[GRADER-ONLY] last_season_quote.pdf is a real font-embedding PDF (browser-printed, not hand-authored, so it converts), it carries two placed raster blocks so the converted document exposes usable graphic frames, and its text flow contains an email address on its own line in the MIDDLE of the flow — the run type observed to be dropped by the inventory tool while its line break is preserved, leaving the summary well-formed and every later offset wrong by a fixed amount.
[GRADER-ONLY] Print resolution requested at the merge step is silently ignored; only a separate render step delivers it.
[GRADER-ONLY] The order of returned per-record raster outputs does not match the row order, and the labels on those outputs assert an order that is wrong.

[GRADER-ONLY] The client asks for material she can change next season. That is a requirement about the form of the handover; a flattened deliverable satisfies the letter of every visual gate and fails the brief.

[GRADER-ONLY] The Express surface exports no files on this host. A poster deliverable that stops at an Express document leaves the client with nothing to send a printer, and the brief explicitly asks for a file the print shop will take.

hardness_rationale:
SPEC PARTITION — READ FIRST. Only these fields are AGENT-FACING: id, brand_name, engagement_title, one_line_ask, client_brief, the input files, brand_identity_additions.price_range / .positioning / .demographics / .competitive_set, and deliverables[].name / .kind / .spec. Everything else in this document — stages[] and all their subtasks and decisions, traps[], failure_gates[], verifiers_auto[], verifiers_human[], brand_identity_additions.design_implication, and this paragraph — is GRADER-ONLY and must never be shown to the agent under test. A build-time lint should fail this spec if any distinctive string from traps[] or failure_gates[] also appears in an agent-facing field. The previous revision shipped its own answer key: it named the planted defects, stated the triage verdict, pre-wrote the price-band rationale it then asked the agent to produce, and let the client pre-authorise the one judgement the recovery stage was supposed to test. All of that is now on this side of the line, and the client brief has been rewritten so that the count of archive files, the identity of the odd one out and the permission to rebuild are all gone.

WHERE THE DIFFICULTY ACTUALLY IS. Not in the surface count. Five authored documents and seventeen pages are an ERROR AMPLIFIER, not a source of depth: after the second surface the authoring recipe adds canvas dimensions and tool calls, not decisions, and this spec does not claim otherwise. What the surfaces buy is that one wrong call early is visible in many places late. Nor is it in the ink plates, which are a masked flat fill applied three times — plumbing once the mark exists, and labelled as such here so no reviewer reads it as craft. The genuine gates are these. (1) A triage with no arithmetic answer: four unlabelled rasters, of which TWO are captures of the same numeral sheet — the good scan has lost two glyphs to ink bleed and the poor phone capture is the only clean source for them, so the correct move is to combine, not to choose. A third is a letter sheet photographed on a bench under uneven warm light with a fold shadow across three glyphs, needing materially different prep from a flat scan. The fourth is a photographed garment that yields nothing traceable, and deciding that — and arguing it, since the client has explicitly NOT pre-authorised rebuilding anything — is the agent's call. (2) A per-glyph craft judgement with no single right answer: for each damaged glyph, recover from the second capture, repair, or redraw to match a house alphabet drawn by the client's father in the nineties. This is not a checklist item, it has no correct-by-construction answer, and it is visible downstream — three of the six club names printed in Stage 8 contain a fold-shadowed letter and one contains a bled numeral. (3) The selection-prompt gate: naming the substrate returns the paper, naming the ink's colour, medium and form returns the strokes, and both are valid masks with plausible pixel counts. (4) A definition-of-done gate the toolchain never mentions: the client's stated primary requirement is that a sign-maker can set a word, which means the alphabet has to arrive as addressable glyphs with metrics, not as a picture of an alphabet — and the Stage 8 name plates are unbuildable without it. (5) Cross-surface consistency: one mark, one type system, one line, one ink set and one prepared image set holding across five documents at eight canvas sizes without becoming a redesign, with two silent type traps riding along (names returned in one form and required in another; numeric weights that are not standard across families). (6) The price band, made load-bearing rather than decorative: at £68–£92 a shirt with a four-figure pack total sold to a volunteer treasurer who cannot reclaim VAT, both the discount register and the boutique register are coherent, well-executed, wrong answers, and the agent must additionally distinguish honest production lead time — required here — from discount urgency, which is disqualifying. (7) The deepest gate, saved for last: the reconstructed quote-sheet layout hands back an inventory of its own contents that drops a run while keeping its line break, so offsets computed from the summary are wrong by a fixed amount, validation returns clean and preparation returns success. Because that defect is a tool behaviour this spec does not control, the verifier grades the DISCIPLINE — offsets reconstructed from the document's own story XML, and every placeholder confirmed present before the merge — so the gate holds whether or not the defect fires on this document, and the reference solution records the observed inventory and the true story string.

SCORING SHAPE. Twenty-four hygiene checks are PRECONDITIONS, not points: fail any one and the submission is not scored at all. An agent handed the trap list can no longer bank a high score on plumbing, because plumbing earns nothing. The score sits on thirteen design checks, all readable from returned geometry, submitted HTML and the merge output without anyone reading a pixel: hero area share and position on the A3, largest type size, the price device's two figures in one band at a sane size ratio, an order-by date inside a derived window with zero discount tokens, invariant overlap across the three social roots, one line string across seven roots, each direction's declared carrier dominating only its own comps and each direction reflowing rather than scaling between its two canvases, the recommendation citing real figures and real buyer behaviour, a real table rather than a text block imitating one, a native-vector durability chart, per-row name plates composed from the delivered glyphs, and a handover that is actually a handover. The agent's only reporting obligation is the parameters it dialed — which it knows because it set them — never a measurement.
why_not_a_vlm_one_shot: A general chat model with an image model attached can describe this engagement; it cannot produce it, and the places it fails are not stylistic. Start with the thing the client actually paid for. Her alphabet exists only as ink on decade-old rasters, and what she needs back is addressable vector glyphs with metrics that a sign-maker can set a word from — glyphs whose counters are open, that carry scaling information, that are free of a ground path nobody told you was there, and that include two numerals destroyed by ink bleed in the best capture and recoverable only from the worst one. A model asked to make that alphabet invents letterforms; the actual job is to decide which of four unlabelled files are the same artefact twice, isolate ink from substrate on a photograph lit unevenly across a workbench, get the mask polarity right, trace, decompose, repair three fold-shadowed letters in a hand that is not yours, and be able to say which ones you rebuilt. None of that is a rendering, and every step of it fails silently. Then look at what has to leave the building: an A3 press file at 3508x4961 that a print shop will take, six A4 sheets at 2480x3508 merged one club per page in spreadsheet order from a reconstructed layout whose native file is gone and whose own inventory lies about its contents, a five-slide deck containing a real table with the client's actual figures and a native-vector chart, three social canvases and two store canvases living as editable documents at their own sizes. Chat output is a picture or a paragraph; not one of those is either. The typography is a licensing problem before it is a taste problem: real licensed faces actually embedded in editable documents, at weights that are not what their names imply, requested under names that differ from the names they were returned under — a model working from memory produces a font name in a caption, not a typeface in a file. The photography must be genuinely licensed, traceable, at camera scale, never enlarged, and vetted frame by frame for a manufacturer mark the toolchain cannot remove and the client has already had a letter about; an invented image fails the brief outright. And it is one engagement, not eleven prompts: the recovery feeds the glyph kit, the glyph kit feeds the direction comps and the six printed name plates, the chosen direction binds the poster, the social set, the store pair, the deck and the quote sheet, and a glyph redrawn badly in the first hour is sitting on a table in front of a committee at the end. Finally, the deliverable the client asked for is editability plus a file her printer will accept, and she said so twice — a flat image, however good it looks, fails on both counts.
connector_doability_note: Every deliverable maps onto a chain verified live on this host on 2026-09-10, nothing draws on the still-impossible list, and the two places the connector genuinely cannot deliver a file are handled in the open rather than hidden. SESSION: adobe_mandatory_init runs before any Adobe tool, then get_account_type (must return 'auth'). STAGE 1: headless upload (asset_initialize_file_upload, curl PUT, asset_finalize_file_upload — no file picker), asset_inline_preview so the model looks before choosing parameters, image_apply_adjustments for divergent per-frame prep, image_select_by_prompt at ink level with returnBbox, image_invert_selection for polarity, image_crop_to_bounds driven by that bbox, image_vectorize. Ink-level selection with counters excluded, the polarity difference and the resulting two-colour trace were all verified on exactly this input class — a printed mark photographed on a surface. No tilt is planted, so image_auto_straighten is not required and is not gated on; its behaviour on paper-on-a-bench is unverified here and the spec deliberately does not depend on it. STAGE 2: hygiene (inject viewBox, delete the full-canvas path[0], neutralise any residual opaque counter fills) and glyph decomposition are local file work on the retrieved SVG; the counter form must be confirmed on a counter-heavy representative input during spec authoring and recorded in the reference solution, and P-02 checks openness at the kit level before any placement rather than six documents later. The ink plates use image_fill_area, whose live schema takes an arbitrary RGB colour plus opacity and a maskURI: image_fill_area({imageURIs:[white ground plate], maskURI:<the single Stage-1 numeral mask>, options:{color:{red,green,blue}, opacity:100}, outputFileType:'png'}). That hits exact flat spot inks, keeps every plate resolving to the one Stage-1 mask, and stays inside the brand's flat-ink register. The earlier 'adjacent-hue only, never a named hex' restriction is deleted: it applied to relative HSL moves, which are a no-op on a neutral two-colour source, and it is not how these plates are made. image_apply_color_overlay is explicitly NOT an alternative — no maskURI, no opacity. STAGE 3: font_recommend per role, font_styles for the true numeric weights, find_fonts to launder every name, then ONE get_fontkit_embed_url returning a working, non-domain-locked Typekit embed. suggest_type_palettes and get_type_palette are not used — not surfaced here — and the pairing is the agent's because font_recommend refuses to pair by design. STAGE 4: asset_search with entityScope StockAsset using SHORT queries and no orientation filter (that filter returns zero hits), asset_license_and_download_stock for genuine camera-scale files, image_apply_adjustments for per-frame correction, image_remove_background with a backgroundColor for the studio ground, image_crop_and_resize for downscale-only reframes with the tradeoffs array checked, and image_generative_expand where a cross-aspect crop would clip the subject. image_generative_expand is the single sanctioned generative exception per the live routing doc, which supersedes REBUILD_GROUND_TRUTH.md line 26 on this host; P-11 and P-12 are split so that a correct expand is not scored as an upscale, and P-23's wording is narrowed to text-to-image, generative fill-by-prompt, AI object removal and background-replace-by-prompt. STAGES 5-7: the Group 2 authoring surface — create_visual_design_express_skill, one self-contained HTML per document, html_export_readiness_skill before EVERY export and every retry, then export_html_to_express, verified via asset_search, asset_get_presigned_urls and asset_inline_preview. Every feature used is on the verified CAN list: mixed canvas sizes in one document, true mm print canvases (297x420mm resolving to 1123x1587), absolute-coordinate placement, inline SVG becoming native editable paths, real tables rendering as display:table-row / table-cell with per-cell backgrounds, per-slide auto titles from headings, and a single Typekit link as the only external stylesheet. Nothing is specified that depends on stroked or outlined type, blurs, blend modes, underlines, multi-column text or stacked shadow layers, all of which drop silently. canvasWidth, canvasHeight and slideSelector are never passed as tool params — they are global overrides that would collapse the mixed-format sets. The authoring skill's delivery question and its template-versus-net-new question are both pre-answered in the client brief in the client's own voice, so the skill's 'unless the user already stated the destination clearly' condition is satisfied and no AskUserQuestion stall is legitimate; the regeneration gate never arms because every root is a fixed canvas carrying its own data-canvas-* attributes. PAYLOAD: every image is base64-embedded as a data: URI because no external address resolves — not even the connector's own photoshop-api.adobe.io outputs — and each photo is downscaled to the pixel width its placement box occupies at the target canvas's own scale, which also keeps every reframe a downscale. Any document exceeding the 70 KB inline advisory is uploaded via asset_initialize_file_upload / asset_finalize_file_upload with media_type text/html and passed to export_html_to_express as a *.adobe.com `url`; per-document budget 1.5 MB, and the deck-scale payload must be confirmed importable by that route during spec authoring. VERIFICATION COVERAGE: the rendition preview returns page one only, so every page carrying a photograph, the recovered mark or the price device is either page one of its document or is additionally exported once as a single-root document purely to obtain a page-one render — cheap, fully headless, no extra capability — and in addition slides[].html is parsed for the four verified silent-failure classes (1x1 placeholder img, color="#00000000", a resolved font-family that is not the intended face, computed left/top outside the declared canvas). POSTER PRESS FILE: authored HTML is printed locally to an A3 PDF with headless Chrome — a browser-printed PDF with embedded font subsets is the form convert_pdf_to_indd accepts, whereas a thin hand-authored PDF fails — then uploaded, convert_pdf_to_indd, then document_render_layout at resolution 300, giving 3508x4961 (A3 at 300 dpi, matching the verified 612x792pt -> 2550x3300 behaviour). No bleed and no press preset are claimed: bleed cannot be introduced from a PDF-derived template and pdfPreset is an undiscoverable closed enum, so both are omitted rather than gated. This also gives the engagement a second, genuinely different production route so the authoring recipe is not simply repeated. STAGE 8: convert_pdf_to_indd on a real browser-printed client PDF that carries at least two placed raster blocks (so generate_indd_mapping_prompt returns a non-empty image_frames array — confirmed at authoring time, and gated by P-17), export_idml, generate_indd_mapping_prompt, the mandatory manual step of reconstructing true story offsets from the unzipped IDML Stories/Story_*.xml Content runs, prepare_indd_merge_template with the WHOLE mapping passed as a JSON string in params.mappingJson, a re-export to confirm every placeholder landed, document_merge_data_layout to application/pdf for the one-club-per-page press file and to application/x-indesign for the per-record branch, then document_render_layout at resolution 300 with createSeparateFiles for correctly-ordered, individually-named sheets. Per-club name plates bind through an @-prefixed CSV column holding bare filenames plus additionalImageFiles keyed to those exact filenames — verified to bind a different image per row. Page size is declared A4 so the 2480x3508 assertion is evaluable. text action replace_all is not used; uid values are the integer page_item_id, never the IDML Self string; insert_at_position rows sharing a uid are listed in descending position order. DELIVERABLE HONESTY: download_design is not surfaced, so the Express documents ARE the editable deliverable and the client exports from Express herself — which is why 'export and handover instructions' is a named deliverable with its own human verifier, why the poster additionally ships as a rendered press file, and why no deliverable kind claims to be a file the connector cannot produce. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED: fill_text (non-deterministic, truncates, leaks label prefixes), animate_design (returns no artifact), create_firefly_board (creates nothing), search_design and any template gallery step (the client has ruled out stock templates), qr_mappings (documented but inert), replace_image (not surfaced), all video and audio (the whole family is async with no poll tool on this host), upscaling, OCR, photo compositing, text-to-image, and any request that the agent read a pixel or a hex — every numeric tolerance in this spec sits on the grader's side.
