brand_identity_additions.price_range: Six-SKU Q3 core range, from 890 to 4,900 rupees per piece (roughly $10 to $59). Plain stud pair 890 (ST-01) · stacking band 1,150 (SB-02) · fine chain bracelet 1,690 (CB-03) · filigree pendant 2,450 (FP-04) · jhumka drops 3,200 (JE-05) · wide cuff 4,900 (OC-06). Average order value 2,850. The modal order is two pieces and skews to the lower half of the range; three-piece orders are roughly a fifth of volume. One published bundle: 'The Everyday Three' (stacking band + fine chain bracelet + filigree pendant), list 5,290, sold at 4,690, a saving of 600. Wholesale is 55% of MRP across the range, giving a stockist 45% margin. No piece crosses 5,000; there is no bespoke, no commission, no made-to-order tier. Prices are displayed with the rupee glyph immediately followed by the figure, Indian comma grouping, no trailing dash, taxes included.
brand_identity_additions.positioning: Hallmarked 925 sterling silver made in-house, sold direct plus a couple of marketplace channels for two years, almost entirely on word of mouth. Everyday pieces bought for oneself or as a small gift, worn daily and worn together. Not bridal, not heirloom, not investment, not collected. Two stockists have approached the brand and it now needs a trade story as well as a consumer one.
brand_identity_additions.demographics: Primary buyer 22 to 34, first or second job, metro and tier-2 salaried or a final-year student with disposable income, largely women plus a growing gifting-for-a-friend segment of any gender. Discretionary spend rather than saved-for spend, decided in one sitting on a phone. Buying occasions: self-reward on payday, a friend's birthday, a first-job gift, festival small-gifting, and replacing a piece that tarnished. Repeat purchase is driven by adding to an existing set rather than trading up. Secondary audience for the trade deck: buyers for small independent retail stores.
brand_identity_additions.competitive_set: Independent online silver labels and studio-craft sellers in the 800 to 5,000 band selling direct plus a couple of generic marketplace channels.
brand_identity_additions.design_implication: *** GRADER-FACING ONLY. THIS FIELD MUST NOT APPEAR IN ANY AGENT-VISIBLE RENDERING OF THIS SPEC. It is the reference answer to the engagement's strategic gate; showing it to the agent converts the gate from judgement to transcription and invalidates VH-01, VH-05 and VH-07. *** The price band decides the whole look and a human judge can see it in ten seconds, but nothing agent-facing names any of the following. The correct derivation, from the supplied facts alone (an 890-to-4,900 band, a 2,850 average order, a published three-piece bundle with a stated saving, a phone-first payday buyer, and a founder reporting that people ask about payment plans and are surprised when they reach a number), is six decisions: (a) the price goes ON the creative, large and confident, on the poster, every social format and every ad unit — a fine-jewellery direction hides price behind an enquiry; (b) pieces are composed together as sets rather than one hero object in a void, because the modal order is two and the published offer is three; (c) the ground is warm, mid-tone and daylit rather than the black-and-gold, high-gloss, deep-shadow vocabulary of fine jewellery; (d) the type system is legible at both A3 and inside a 320x50 mobile banner — the high-contrast neoclassical display serifs that any recommender returns for a 'silver jewellery' brief have hairlines that disintegrate at ad-unit scale and signal a price band ten times higher; (e) the call to action is a direct retail verb naming the offer and the number, not a discovery or enquiry register; (f) the bundle saving is shown, because a stated saving is the only thing in the range that is an offer rather than a price. If the same range were priced 80,000 to 400,000 every one of those six inverts — one piece per frame, no price, black ground, hairline serif, vast negative space, an appointment CTA. That inversion is what VH-01's blind comparison against the supplied fine-jewellery control fixture measures, and the six criteria above are the judge's rubric, supplied to the judge and to nobody else.

client_brief:
Hi — thanks for taking this on, and sorry it's a big one. It's really one job but it's been sitting in pieces for months and I'd rather hand the whole thing to one person than keep stitching it together myself.

We're Rukmini Silverworks. Hallmarked 925 sterling, made in-house, everyday pieces. Six of them go live as our Q3 core range next month and this is all for that. Everything's in the folder: the shoot, the catalogue with codes and prices, the shot list, our brand sheet, the copy my sister wrote, and last year's hangtag as a PDF.

Where we are. Two years selling direct from our own store and a couple of marketplace channels, almost entirely on word of mouth. Pieces run 890 to 4,900. Average order is about 2,850 — most people buy two at a time, some three, and we publish one bundle. Buyers are 22 to 34, first or second job, buying for themselves on payday or for a friend's birthday. They decide in one sitting, on a phone.

Why I'm hiring, and I'll be blunt because it's the whole problem: the work photographs beautifully and it does not sell. People message us asking whether we do payment plans. Someone asked last month if we take a deposit. When they finally get to a number they're surprised, and by then most of them have already gone. And two stockists have asked what our range and pricing actually looks like and I've been sending them a spreadsheet like an idiot. Something about how we present ourselves is doing this and I can't see it from the inside. That's what I'm paying you to fix.

The product shots need to become usable. They're straight off the card — we shot over two afternoons in the studio at the back. Put them in a row on the store and they don't look like they belong to the same range, which is embarrassing. I need them looking like one shoot, clean on white for the store listings, and cut out from their backgrounds so we can drop them into anything else you build. There's a little grey step card at the edge of the sweep in every frame. Do whatever you need with it — just never let it end up in anything a customer sees.

I need our mark back. We lost the original artwork when our old designer went quiet on us and stopped answering; all we have left is a photo of the letterpress proof and a photo of the stamped metal tag we press into the pouches. That mark is the only piece of us that's stayed constant and I want it back as real artwork we can scale, recolour and put on a dark background without it looking like a photograph of a logo. It has to hold at the size it prints on a hangtag and at the size it sits on a poster.

Show me options before you build anything. Three directions, side by side in one place so I can look across them rather than have them explained to me one at a time. Then tell me which one you'd actually run, and why. I trust your pick — send me the three and your recommendation, but don't wait on me, start building in your recommended direction the same day. If I hate it I'll say so and we'll adjust.

Then build it out. Here's what I need.

A poster for the pop-up market stall, A3. My print shop pulls the file straight out of my Express account, so what I need from you is that it's right and that it's editable in there — I'll handle the printing myself. The stall is on a busy aisle and it has to stop somebody from ten feet away, so put the pieces on a solid block of colour rather than floating them over a photograph. Stall details are on the brand sheet.

The social set — the square for feed, the taller portrait one, a full-screen story, and a wide one for the shop header, plus one more square that's about the pricing. They're all different shapes and I don't want the same picture squashed five ways; when you send them, tell me what you decided to do differently in each one.

The ad units. We're running paid traffic for the first time. The agency quoted me three slots: the medium rectangle, the little mobile banner that sits under the fold, and the half-page. Nearly everyone who buys from us is on a phone, so those have to work small.

A short deck for the stockists. Six slides, no more. Open with our mark, say who we are and what we charge, and then answer the things the two shops actually asked me — what it costs them, what they make on it, minimum order, how long we take to ship, how we restock, and what it arrives in. The pricing has to be readable as a table, not prose. Don't put the three directions in this one; that's for me, not for them.

And the hangtags. Every piece ships with the same little card. Last year I paid someone to typeset six separate files by hand, which was mad. I've attached last year's card so you can see the layout. One print file this time, one card per piece, all six, so I can send it straight to the printer.

A few rules. No faces, no hands, no models anywhere — we've never shot people and I don't want to start, it changes what the brand is. We've always shot on stone offcuts and folded linen; show the pieces together on a surface, that's how we've always done it, just no people in it. Anything you hand back has to be genuinely editable by us afterwards, in files we can open and change ourselves — I've been burned by flat pictures I had to come back and pay for every time a price moved. And tell me plainly what I can change myself and what I have to come back to you for; I'd rather know now.

Everything has to tell somebody where to buy. The store address and our handle are on the brand sheet, and so are the stall dates. Put a code on the poster and on the hangtag that takes people straight to the store.

If you need a surface or a texture, buy something properly licensed and bill it to me — keep it to two or three, materials and surfaces only, nothing with a person in it, and nothing over about 4,000 all in. Send me the receipts. Send me the reference you're pulling from too, I like seeing where it comes from — half a dozen images, not fifty.

Fee is 95,000 for the lot plus the stock at cost. Three and a half weeks. Send me the three directions as soon as you have them.

stages.name: S1 — Intake, look, and a committed treatment plan (checkpoint 1 of 4 begins)
stages.goal: Get every client file into the working environment, actually look at each one, and commit in writing to a per-piece preparation plan and a per-capture source decision before any pixel is touched.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. The triage, and it is deferred-consequence by construction. The six frames are neutrally named, superficially identical sweep shots; the shot list binds a frame to a catalogue row and nothing more. Nothing tells the agent that a pierced openwork pendant and a pair of fully separated jhumka drops behave differently under automatic subject isolation than a stud, a band, a chain or a cuff do. The agent has to reason from what it sees — eleven enclosed apertures on FP-04, two detached components on JE-05 — to a per-piece route, and record it now, because S4 and S5 consume it. Correct answer: ST-01, SB-02, CB-03 and OC-06 are safe as free transparent cutouts (their gaps are all open to the outer ground); FP-04 and JE-05 must instead be delivered as panel-matched plates whose ground value is not yet known, because it is chosen in S4. The same judgement applies to the two mark captures, which arrive as two same-extension rasters with neutral names: capture_01 is a flat, evenly-lit, coloured-ink letterpress proof and is the only viable trace source; capture_02 is a same-metal debossed tag readable only through relief, and the correct outcome is to reject it as a trace source and retain it as a weight reference for the reduced stamp. The agent must also notice, unprompted, that one frame is off-axis and that the studio reference wedge is present in all six.
subtasks: Every client file is in the working environment and has been looked at before any decision is recorded.
A written, per-piece plan exists saying how each of the six will be prepared for reuse, and why that route was chosen for that specific piece.
A written call on which of the two mark captures is the artwork source and what the other one is actually good for.
A note on anything present in the frames that must be kept for internal reference but must never reach anything a customer sees.
A note on any frame that will not sit correctly alongside the others as supplied.
The plan is explicit about which prepared assets depend on a decision not yet made, and says which decision.
stages.feeds_into: S2 (preparation route per piece), S3 (which capture is the trace source), S4 (which pieces make the panel value load-bearing), S5 (where a wrong S1 call first becomes visible)

stages.name: S2 — Studio pass: one shoot out of two afternoons, then store-ready imagery
stages.goal: Make six differently-lit frames read as a single shoot against one silver white point, rectify the off-axis frame, and produce both the retained reference-bearing masters and the clean 1600x1600 white-ground store tiles with the studio reference cropped away.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. Per-frame divergent correction by eye toward one agreed look. One global setting applied to all six, or a per-frame automatic tone pass, both return success and both visibly fail to match — the two warm frames stay warm, the cool frame stays cool and the dark frame stays dark relative to the others. The agent must dial each frame separately toward the neutral step wedge and report the parameters it chose per image. It must also rectify the 2.4-degree rotation on sku_04 BEFORE any tonal or isolation work, since the crop bounds derive from it, and it must resist reaching for a tile larger than the source honestly allows. The safe operation order is neutralise, then straighten, then isolate or fill, then crop to padded bounds from the selection's returned bbox, then downscale to 1600x1600 LAST — because background removal silently downscales oversized inputs and reports it only in a tradeoffs entry, after which a naive final resize will silently interpolate up to its 2x cap to hit the target.
subtasks: The six frames read as one shoot against a common silver white point when placed in a row on a listing page.
Six 1600x1600 white-ground store tiles, consistent piece scale and breathing room across all six, with nothing from the studio setup visible in any of them.
The six corrected full-frame masters are retained as internal reference with the studio reference still in shot.
One reusable prepared asset per piece, in the form the S1 plan committed to, with the pieces that depend on a later decision held in a state that can still take it.
A written shot-treatment sheet recording what was done to each frame, so the next person who shoots for the brand can match it.
Nothing anywhere in the chain is larger than the source honestly allows.
stages.feeds_into: S5 and S6 (every prepared piece used in poster, social, ads, deck), S8 (the shot-treatment sheet and the asset index)

stages.name: S3 — Recover the mark once, clean it, and build the family everything else reuses (checkpoint 1 ends)
stages.goal: Turn a photograph of a lost logo into genuine scalable artwork: one master vector of the full lockup, hygienic enough to sit on a dark ground and to be recoloured, plus the colourway and size family the rest of the engagement draws on.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. Four separate craft decisions, each with an invisible failure mode. (1) How to name what it wants isolated: asking for the emblem on the proof sheet pulls the sheet; naming the marking by its own visual properties — its colour, its medium, its stroke character — pulls the ink. (2) That a compound lockup must be reached PER ELEMENT: a single selection over emblem-plus-wordmark-plus-rule is verified to come back unreliably partial, silently dropping an inner rule or a central element, and the result looks entirely correct in isolation. The master is therefore assembled once from separate per-element extractions, not lifted in one pass. (3) Polarity before tracing: both polarities trace successfully, one yields a positive outline with counters and interior detail open, the other yields a full-canvas dark plate with the mark knocked out of it. (4) Post-trace hygiene nobody prompts for: the trace arrives with an opaque full-bleed rectangle as its first path and with no coordinate system, so it will neither scale nor composite — and both defects are invisible against white and catastrophic on the deck's dark cover. The client explicitly asked to be able to recolour the mark, so the deliverable is a colourway family, not one positive artwork.
subtasks: One master artwork of the mark exists as real scalable vector, assembled once, with its interior detail open and every element of the lockup present.
It sits correctly on a dark field and on a light field with no box, plate or halo behind it, and this has been checked against a dark field rather than assumed.
A colourway family is derived from that one master: the primary positive, a one-colour reversed version for dark grounds, and a one-colour solid black version for the print file.
A size family is derived from the same master: horizontal lockup, mark alone, and a reduced stamp form.
It holds at hangtag size and at poster size.
A written note of which variant is authorised for which surface, and why.
stages.feeds_into: S4 (appears in all three directions), S5 (poster, all five social artboards, all three ad units), S6 (deck cover on a dark ground — where a bad recovery is most visible), S7 (the stamp form, rasterised, in the hangtag's graphic frame)

stages.name: S4 — Type system, palette, licensed surfaces, three directions and an argued recommendation (checkpoint 2 begins)
stages.goal: Build a real type system and palette for the brand, license two or three material surfaces that obey the no-people rule and the stated budget, present three genuinely distinct art directions side by side in one editable document, and commit to one in writing.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. Three decisions, and the price band governs all of them, unprompted. First, typography: any recommender fed a silver-jewellery brief returns the fine-jewellery drawer — high-contrast neoclassical display serifs with hairline strokes — and it explicitly refuses to pair a heading face with a body face or to warn that those hairlines disintegrate inside a 320x50 mobile banner. The agent owns the shortlist, the pairing, the roles, the sizes and the numeric weights, and owns whether the type it picked belongs to an 890-rupee stud or to a house selling at fifty times that. It must also launder every font name into canonical form before requesting a kit, because one bad or wrongly-cased name kills the entire kit including every valid face in the same request, and it must address families by the slug the kit returns rather than by the name it asked for, because the requested name silently falls back. Second, the palette: the agent must fix the exact value of the solid colour field the client asked for and the exact value of the deck's dark field, and write both down, because S5's panel-matched plates are worthless unless their fill equals the panel they land on. Third, the recommendation: three directions must be materially different propositions rather than one layout in three colourways, and the pick must be defended against the range, the average order, the published bundle saving and the founder's reported symptom — a recommendation argued from aesthetics alone fails this gate even when the pick happens to be right.
subtasks: A type system with defined roles, chosen and paired by the studio, that has to work at poster scale and inside the smallest ad slot the agency quoted.
A palette, including the exact value of the solid colour field the client asked for and the exact value of the deck's dark field, written down before anything is built on it.
Two or three licensed material surfaces, no people, nothing AI-generated, inside the stated budget, with the receipts.

Three genuinely different directions in one editable document the client can look across, each fully realised with the recovered mark, at least one prepared piece, live type in the licensed faces, the palette and a real price treatment.
A reference board of about half a dozen images, shareable.
The exported result has been looked at and corrected before it is presented.
A written recommendation naming one direction and arguing it from who buys from this brand and what they pay.
stages.feeds_into: S2/S5 handoff (the panel value the held-back pieces are filled with), S5 and S6 (locked type, palette, chosen direction), S8 (the font provenance record)

stages.name: S5 — Campaign build: A3 poster, five-format social set, three display ad units (checkpoint 2 ends)
stages.goal: Execute the chosen direction across every surface the client asked for, as client-editable documents, with the recovered mark, the prepared pieces, the locked type system, the catalogue's real prices and the brand's destination carried consistently across all nine artboards.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. First, the consequence of S1 lands here: the two pieces flagged as unsafe for free transparency must now be filled to the exact panel value locked in S4, and that only pays off if the two values agree — knock them to white in S2 and drop them onto a coloured panel and every piece sits in a visible white rectangle. Second, composition under the price band at wildly different scales: how a direction designed at A3 survives a 600x500 rectangle and a 640x100 mobile banner — what is dropped, what is promoted, whether the price and the mark still read — and how each of five differently-shaped social canvases gets its own composition rather than one image squashed five ways. Third, how a set is shown without people: the client's own answer is a surface, so sets are built by arranging the prepared per-piece assets at coordinates over a licensed surface, never by combining two photographs, which is not a capability that exists. Fourth, every photographic element must be embedded rather than referenced, because an external URL — including one produced by the imaging tools themselves — is silently substituted and arrives as an empty box while the export reports success; and a data URI in a CSS background is dropped outright, leaving an empty div with geometry and no image at all.
subtasks: An A3 poster at true physical dimensions, editable, with a licensed surface, the mark, a set composition, the offer and the destination.
One editable document holding the whole social set — feed square, portrait, full-screen story, wide shop header, and a pricing square — each at its own native size inside that single document.
One editable document holding all three ad units at the sizes the agency quoted, with type composed for those canvases rather than scaled down from the poster.
A stated composition rule per social format, saying what was dropped, what was promoted and what the crop centres on.
At least one composition arranges three pieces together.
Two competing headline-and-call-to-action treatments for the primary feed square, with one chosen and the choice explained, before it is carried across the rest of the set.
Every photographic element actually renders in the delivered document, verified rather than assumed.
Prices, the offer and the destination are carried identically across every surface.
stages.feeds_into: S6 (the deck shows this work and must not contradict it), S8 (proof and handover)

stages.name: S6 — Six-slide stockist deck (checkpoint 3 begins)
stages.goal: One editable six-slide 1920x1080 document that answers what a retail buyer actually asked: the mark on a dark cover, who the brand is and what it charges, a real price and margin table, the trade terms, the range grouped the way people buy, and the rollout.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. What a stockist needs versus what a designer wants to show. The client explicitly excluded the three directions from this deck, so the slide a designer would reach for first is banned and the slot has to be filled with trade information instead — minimum order, lead time, replenishment and packaging. The price architecture has to be legible as structure rather than prose and has to carry MRP, wholesale and margin side by side, which is a harder table than a list of prices and is the thing the buyer is actually deciding on. The rollout slide has to carry a real drawn chart as editable vector rather than a picture of one. And the cover is the moment the recovered mark meets a dark ground, so every shortcut taken in S3 — a substrate-shaped blob, an inverted plate, an un-stripped backing rectangle, a positive artwork used where a reversed one was needed — surfaces here and nowhere earlier.
subtasks: Cover: the recovered mark on the campaign's dark field, in the right colourway for a dark field.
Positioning: the band, the buyer and the order behaviour in the brand's own voice.
Price architecture as a genuine table — every piece with its code, finish, retail price, wholesale price and margin, plus the bundle and its saving.
Trade terms — minimum order, lead time, replenishment and what it ships in, including the hangtag.
The range, using the prepared pieces, grouped the way people actually buy.
Rollout, carrying a real drawn chart as editable vector rather than an image of one.
The export produced six distinct artboards, each correctly titled, and this has been confirmed rather than assumed.
stages.feeds_into: S8 (proof and handover)

stages.name: S7 — Hangtag print run from last year's card (checkpoint 3 ends)
stages.goal: Turn the client's flat PDF of last year's hangtag into a live personalised template driven by the catalogue, and deliver one print file containing all six cards, one piece per card, plus high-resolution proofs for sign-off.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. How to bind fields into a document that was never built to be merged, and whether to trust the tooling's own account of what the card says. The converted template carries no field markers, and the structural summary offered of each frame's text is lossy: it can omit an entire text run while keeping that run's line break, so the string still looks well-formed and every character offset after it is wrong by the length of the omission. The mapping then validates clean, reports success, and silently ships six cards missing two fields — a failure invisible in every tool response and visible only on the merged file. The correct move is to open the document, reconstruct each frame's true story text from the document's own content runs, compute offsets from that, and then confirm the placeholders actually landed rather than accepting a success message. The agent must also decide what to do with the recovered mark on this surface, since a vector cannot be bound as a merge image and the mark is identical on all six cards, and it must decide what it can and cannot honestly promise a printer from a source like this.
subtasks: Last year's card becomes an editable layout document whose real structure has been inspected — every frame, every text run, every existing placement.
The true content of each frame has been established from the document itself before any mapping is computed.
Piece name, price, code and finish come off the catalogue onto the card, and the recovered mark sits in the card's graphic frame.
The purity line and the care line are on every card as fixed copy.
The prepared template genuinely carries every intended field, confirmed rather than reported.
One print file, six pages, one piece per page, in catalogue order.
High-resolution proofs at true print resolution for client sign-off.
A plain statement of what this source can and cannot be asked to deliver to a printer.
stages.feeds_into: S8 (proof and handover)

stages.name: S8 — Proof, self-correct, and hand over (checkpoint 4)
stages.goal: Look at everything produced the way the client will look at it, fix what is broken, and hand over a package she can actually operate without coming back.
stages.decision_the_agent_must_make: GRADER-FACING. What to reject in its own work, and how to check it honestly given that only the first artboard of a multi-artboard document can be rendered back for inspection. The correct discipline is to have checked the pixel-level questions upstream on the assets themselves — where each prepared piece can be previewed directly — and to check the layouts structurally, reading the importer's own returned representation of every artboard for empty or placeholder images, off-canvas coordinates, collapsed widths and wrong resolved typefaces, with a throwaway single-artboard export where a genuine visual check is unavoidable. An agent that claims it visually verified all six deck slides from one rendition preview has claimed something the tooling does not do. It also has to decide what the client needs written down so a price change next quarter does not require re-hiring, and to be honest about the one deliverable she cannot re-run herself.
subtasks: Every produced document has been checked and anything that arrived empty, displaced, off-canvas, invisible or in the wrong typeface has been corrected and re-exported.
The same mark, type system, palette, price convention and destination carry across poster, social set, ad units, deck and hangtag with no drift.
The shot-treatment sheet is complete and reflects genuinely different decisions per frame.
An asset index maps every prepared or recovered element to every surface it appears on.
The direction rationale is written and argued from who buys and what they pay.

A source handover exists: the authored sources for every layout, the vector masters and their colourways, the merge template and the catalogue, and a named font list with the exact families and numeric weights used.
A one-page note on changing a price, distinguishing what the client can do herself from what has to come back, and stating what she needs to hold in order to edit these files at all.
A plain statement of anything that was asked for and cannot honestly be promised.
stages.feeds_into: final delivery

deliverables.spec: The authored sources for every layout; the vector masters and all three colourways; the merge template and the catalogue CSV; a named font list with exact families, kit identifier and the numeric weights used; the shot-treatment sheet; an asset index mapping every prepared element to every surface it appears on; the direction rationale; a one-page 'how to change a price' distinguishing edit-it-yourself from come-back-to-us; a prerequisites line stating what the client must hold to open and edit these files; and a plain statement of anything asked for that cannot honestly be promised.
deliverables.built_from: the whole engagement

options_required: Three places, escalating in consequence. (1) Stage 4 is the formal options gate: three genuinely distinct art directions, authored as three artboards inside one document so the client can compare across rather than down, each fully realised with the recovered mark, a prepared piece, live licensed type, the palette and a real price treatment — not three colourways of one layout, and not two straw men and a favourite. The agent must then commit to one and defend it in writing against the range, the average order value, the published bundle and its saving, and the founder's reported symptom. A recommendation argued from aesthetics alone fails this gate even if the pick happens to be right. The client has pre-authorised the agent to proceed on its own recommendation the same day, so there is no approval stall — but the recommendation must still exist as a written argument, and it is graded as one. (2) Inside Stage 4 the type decision is itself an options problem the tooling refuses to solve: a recommender returns roughly thirty candidates per role in named buckets and explicitly declines to pair a heading face with a body face or to comment on how a face behaves at small sizes. The agent must generate its own shortlist per role, pair, assign roles, sizes and family-specific numeric weights, and justify the pairing against the smallest canvas in the set as well as the largest — a face that carries the A3 poster and dies in a 320x50 banner is the wrong pick, and the agent only discovers that by considering the whole set before committing. (3) Stage 5 requires two competing headline-and-call-to-action treatments for the primary feed square, written by the agent from the client's raw copy deck (which contains no ready-made retail CTA and no price-forward line), with one chosen and the choice explained, before it is carried into the rest of the set.
element_reuse: The brand mark is recovered exactly ONCE — assembled once, in Stage 3, from per-element extractions off a single photographed proof — and everything else in the engagement draws on that one master. Because the supplied capture is a compound lockup (emblem, rule, wordmark), a single selection over the whole thing comes back unreliably partial, so the master is composited from separately extracted, separately traced, separately cleaned elements; that assembly happens once and never again. From it come three colourways (primary positive, one-colour reversed, one-colour solid black) and three size forms (horizontal lockup, mark alone, reduced stamp), plus one rasterised transparent PNG of the stamp at print scale for the merge surface. Those variants then appear on all three direction artboards, on the A3 poster, on all five social artboards, on all three ad units, on the deck's dark cover and its range slide, and — through an entirely different production surface — in the hangtag's graphic frame on all six merged cards. Roughly twenty-five placements, one source. This is deliberately structured so the cost of a Stage 3 shortcut is paid everywhere at once, and paid late: if the extraction names the substrate instead of the marking, every surface carries a sheet-shaped grey box; if the lockup is lifted in one pass, every surface carries a mark with a component silently missing; if polarity is wrong before tracing, every surface carries a dark rectangle; if the backing path is not stripped and no coordinate system is injected, the mark looks fine on white store tiles and fine on the poster's light margin and then arrives on the deck cover as a pale box on a dark field; and if only a positive colourway is produced, the dark cover gets a positive mark with a lightened fill instead of a proper reversed one. The second reuse spine is the prepared piece set: six pieces prepared once in Stage 2 and reused across store tiles, poster, five social formats, three ad units and the deck's range slide — with the wrinkle that the preparation route chosen in Stage 1 determines whether that reuse survives contact with a coloured ground, and the value it must be filled with is not chosen until Stage 4. The third is the catalogue: the same six prices, the same wholesale figures and the same bundle saving drive the poster, the pricing square, the ad units, the deck's price table and the merged hangtags, so a price that drifts between surfaces is a real and checkable inconsistency. The fourth is the destination: one store address, one handle, one scannable code, byte-identical everywhere it appears.
failure_gates: Designing for the wrong price band. The subject matter pulls hard toward fine jewellery and any type recommender fed a silver-jewellery brief returns the fine-jewellery drawer. Nothing agent-facing names the correction; the client reports only a symptom (people ask about payment plans; they are surprised when they reach a number) and a set of facts (an 890-to-4,900 band, a 2,850 average order, a published three-piece bundle with a stated saving, a phone-first payday buyer). An agent that follows the recommender ships a look ten times the brand's price for a 2,450-rupee pendant: one lonely piece per frame, no price on the creative, a discovery-register call to action, and hairlines that disintegrate in a 320x50 banner. Visible to a briefed judge in ten seconds against the supplied control fixture.

Naming the substrate instead of the marking when isolating the logo. Asking for the emblem on the proof sheet returns the sheet; naming the marking by its own colour, medium and stroke character returns the ink. The wrong wording produces a plausible-looking, correctly-sized, entirely useless sheet-shaped region, and every downstream trace, variant and placement inherits it.

Lifting a compound lockup in one selection. Emblem-plus-rule-plus-wordmark comes back partial — an inner rule or a central element silently dropped — and the result looks entirely correct in isolation and at thumbnail size. The correct route is per-element extraction assembled once into one master.

Choosing the wrong capture as the trace source. One is a flat, evenly-lit, coloured-ink impression on a distinct substrate; the other is a same-metal debossed marking readable only through relief and raking shadow. They arrive as two same-extension rasters with neutral names.

Getting polarity wrong before tracing. Both polarities trace successfully. One yields a positive outline with counters and interior detail open; the other yields a full-canvas dark plate with the mark knocked out of it. The difference is one call and it is not visible until the mark is placed on colour.

Skipping post-trace hygiene. The trace ships with an opaque full-bleed first path and no coordinate system. Left as-is it will not scale and it composites as a solid box — invisible on white store tiles and on a light poster margin, catastrophic on the deck's dark cover. An agent that only ever checks its mark against white never finds out.

Delivering only a positive colourway. The client asked explicitly to be able to recolour the mark and put it on a dark background, and the deck cover is dark. A positive artwork with a lightened fill is not a reversed mark, and the print file needs a single-plate black.

Treating all six pieces as one preparation problem. Automatic subject isolation returns success on all six but recovers an outer silhouette only: a pierced openwork pendant comes back with eleven apertures filled by the captured sweep, and a pair of fully separated earrings loses a component because subject detection wants one coherent blob. Both defects are invisible on a white store tile — pale fill on a white ground — and glaring the moment the same asset lands on the campaign's colour field or the deck's dark slide.

Reaching for background removal where a masked fill is required. Background removal isolates the outer ground only and cannot punch an enclosed interior hole, so setting a ground colour on the openwork pendant replaces the outer sweep and leaves eleven pale apertures behind. The route that actually works is a positive selection of the piece by its own form and material, inverted, then a masked solid fill in the locked value — which fills the outer ground and the apertures with the same exact value in one pass, as PNG.

Locking the fill value before locking the palette, or failing to make the two agree. Fill to white in Stage 2 and place on a coloured panel and every piece sits in a visible white rectangle; fill to a colour chosen before the direction was decided and every piece sits in a subtly wrong halo. Choosing a near-neutral panel to make the two trivially agree is separately caught by the chroma floor.

One global correction, or a per-frame automatic pass, across six differently-lit frames. Both report success, and both leave the two warm frames warm, the cool frame cool and the dark frame dark relative to the rest. The six then sit in a row on the store looking like exactly what they are — two afternoons, not one shoot.

Correcting tone before rectifying the off-axis frame, or resizing before cropping. Background removal silently downscales oversized inputs and reports it only in a tradeoffs entry; a final resize then silently interpolates up to a 2x cap to reach the target tile, shipping enlarged pixels with no other signal.

Referencing photographic material by URL in an authored layout. Every external image URL — including output URLs produced by the imaging tools themselves — is silently substituted and arrives as an empty box while the export reports success.

Putting a photograph in a CSS background rather than an image element. A background image with an embedded payload is dropped entirely: the element arrives with its full geometry and no image at all, and there is no image element left to detect.

Writing type by the name it asked for rather than the name the embed returns, and assuming a weight. The embedded family is addressed by a different string than the one requested, so the requested name silently falls back to a default face; and numeric weights are family-specific, so a reflexive value can land two cuts away from the intended one with no warning anywhere. Both failures are invisible in the source and visible in the output.

Collapsing a multi-artboard document into one artboard, or flattening a mixed-size set to a single canvas size. The five-format social set, the three-unit ad set and the six-slide deck each depend on the document declaring its own per-artboard structure and sizes; naming the wrapper instead of the per-artboard class, or passing global canvas dimensions, silently produces one artboard or N wrong-shaped ones and still reports success.

Claiming visual verification the tooling cannot provide. Only the first artboard of a multi-artboard document renders back for inspection. An agent that asserts it looked at all six deck slides that way has claimed something false; the honest discipline is asset-level preview upstream plus structural inspection of every artboard's returned representation.

Trusting the summarised description of the hangtag's contents instead of establishing what the card actually says. The summary can omit a whole text run while keeping its line break, so the string still looks well-formed and every offset after it is wrong. The mapping then validates clean, reports success, and silently ships six cards missing fields.

Composing for one piece when the modal order is two and the published offer is three. A single hero object on an empty ground is correct for the price band above this one. At this band the set composition is the proposition, and its absence is a strategy error visible on every surface.

Shipping creative with nowhere to go. A stall poster with no dates and no address, and display units with a call to action pointing nowhere, are not launchable; a media agency returns them the same afternoon.
Promising the printer something this source cannot deliver — bleed on a template derived from a flat PDF, or a named press standard — instead of stating the limitation plainly.
traps: Automatic background isolation cannot open enclosed negative space: eleven pierced apertures stay filled with captured sweep at full reported success, and setting a background colour changes only the outer ground.
Automatic background isolation needs one coherent subject: a pair of separated earrings loses a component, and the surviving half looks entirely correct in isolation and on a white tile.
Selection prompts that name the object a graphic sits ON return the object, not the graphic. The failure produces a well-formed mask of the wrong thing.
A single selection over a compound lockup comes back unreliably partial, dropping an inner element while reporting success.
A debossed same-metal marking offers no colour or medium handle for a prompt-driven selection; it is a reference, not a trace source.
Selection masks are hard binary with no soft edge; any edge quality in a delivered asset has to come from the isolation route, not from the selection.
Tracing a mask in the wrong polarity yields a full-canvas dark plate that reports success and reads as a mark at thumbnail size.
Every trace ships with an opaque full-canvas backing path as its first element and no coordinate system, so it neither scales nor composites — and both defects are invisible against white.

Background removal silently downscales oversized inputs and discloses it only in a tradeoffs entry; the crop-and-resize tool will then silently enlarge up to a 2x cap to reach the requested target, also disclosed only in a tradeoffs entry.

A background-colour knockout returns JPEG, whose compression artefacts around a high-contrast silver piece read as exactly the halo a coloured-ground placement is judged on — while a string-equality check on the declared value passes regardless.
Subject-aware extraction crops mis-frame on sparse artwork while reporting a plausible result and a low confidence value nobody reads.

External image URLs in authored layouts — including URLs produced by the imaging tools themselves — are silently replaced by a transparent placeholder that keeps the element's full geometry; the export reports success and the page renders empty boxes.
An embedded payload inside a CSS background image is dropped entirely, leaving a geometry-only element with no image element to detect.

Embedded photography inflates the authored payload fast; a photo-heavy poster crosses the advisory inline size threshold and needs the hosted route, which the agent must recognise rather than push through.
Font kits are all-or-nothing: one unlaundered or wrongly-cased name kills the entire kit including every valid face in the same request.
The string used to address an embedded family is not the string used to request it; using the requested name produces a silent fallback with no error anywhere.
Numeric weights are family-specific, so the reflexive value can resolve to a lighter or heavier cut than intended, silently — and the resulting hairline is exactly what fails at ad-unit scale.
The importer's own default family is itself a real, entitled, plausible-looking face, so a total type-system collapse is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice unless font provenance is recorded.
Semantic markup does not carry weight into the export; anything not explicitly styled loses its emphasis.

Naming the wrapper rather than the per-artboard class collapses an N-artboard document to one, and passing global canvas dimensions as parameters overrides every artboard's own declared size and destroys a mixed-format set.
Right- and bottom-anchored elements without explicit dimensions collapse and run off the canvas edge, clipped, while the export reports success.

A range of decorative treatments are dropped silently — outlines, stroked text, blurs, blend modes, text shadows, all but the first layer of a multi-layer shadow, multi-column text, underline — and stroked-and-transparent text becomes fully invisible.
Elements outside the artboard roots are excluded entirely, which is useful for scaffolding and destructive if a real element drifts outside.
The rendition preview returns the first artboard only, so a multi-artboard document cannot be visually verified page by page that way.

The structural summary of a converted print template is lossy: a whole text run can be omitted while its line break is kept, so the string still looks well-formed and every offset after it is wrong. The mapping then validates clean, reports success, and silently drops fields.
A converted PDF only exposes a mappable graphic frame if the source PDF contained a placed raster; a continuous text-only flow collapses to a single frame with nothing to map separately.
Merge output ordering is not trustworthy for every output format, and resolution requested at merge time is silently ignored — true print resolution requires the separate render step.
A vector cannot be bound as a merge image, and a variable per-record code is documented but inert — it validates, reports success and produces nothing.
Bleed cannot be introduced into a template derived from a flat PDF, and named press presets are rejected outright.
A near-neutral panel colour makes the fill-value agreement check pass trivially while hiding every isolation defect the coloured ground exists to expose.
